text:
FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WANE) — This summer, Indiana Governor Mike Braun put the message out to the state of Indiana. Nuclear power is the future.

The Indiana Advanced Nuclear Ready Communities Program launched in July and is asking communities to advance nuclear energy development. It is designed to get communities ready to build nuclear reactors or small modular reactors (SMRs).

Right now, the page on the state’s website uses a picture of Fort Wayne’s skyline to encourage communities to join the program, but the city tells WANE 15 that, at this time, they are “reviewing the state’s program.”

A Monday statement from Fort Wayne Mayor (D) Sharon Tucker reads as follows.

We’re always looking at what’s best for Fort Wayne’s long-term energy future and economic growth. Our team is reviewing the state’s program to understand what it would mean for our community, our workforce, and our infrastructure. We haven’t made any decisions, but we believe in staying at the table for conversations that could bring investment and good jobs to our region.

(D) Mayor Sharon Tucker, Fort Wayne

AEP is already pursuing an SMR at the Rockport Plant in Spencer County, Indiana, meaning Fort Wayne would likely not be one of the first adopters of nuclear power in the state even if it got involved tomorrow.

WANE 15 reached out to the county about participating as well but has yet to hear back.

At Hartford's Swift Factory, the North Hartford Partnership recently selected consultants who will assess climate risks, conduct site analyses, engage community members, and identify funding opportunities for the proposed hubs.

The resilience hubs are intended to serve some of Connecticut's most climate-vulnerable neighborhoods, providing resources before, during, and after extreme weather events.

"This is about 10,000 square feet of space that we're looking to build out as soon as funding becomes available," said Brenda Watson of the North Hartford Partnership while discussing a potential hub location in Hartford's North End.

Organizers say the hubs would focus on emergency preparedness, energy equity, and economic resilience, while also creating pathways to green jobs and clean energy technologies.

"For disproportionately impacted areas, we are creating solutions for them to deal with things like too much sun, too much heat, too much cold, too much rain, too much flooding," explains Andrea Hawkins with Leading Culture Solutions, one of the consulting agencies.

North Hartford has been identified as an area particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts, including urban heat island effects and flash flooding from heavy rainfall.

In addition to serving as community gathering spaces during emergencies, organizers envision the hubs helping residents access clean energy technologies and programs that could lower utility costs and improve health outcomes.

"And in quiet times like now, be able to help the community access clean and green technology that would help reduce their energy burden and improve their health and economic outcomes," Watson said.

Supporters say the hubs could help residents better withstand extreme heat, severe storms, power outages, and rising energy costs while ensuring resources are distributed equitably throughout the community.

"Making sure that we're doing the things that we need to do to be sure that everyone can access, have equitable access to all of those resources," Hawkins said.

Following the planning phase, project partners will move into design and community engagement efforts while seeking additional funding to bring the resilience hubs from concept to reality.

text:
Three environmental organizations are threatening to sue the developers of two West San Antonio data centers, alleging the companies improperly used streamlined state permits to avoid stricter federal air-pollution requirements.

The Environmental Integrity Project, Sierra Club and Public Citizen sent a formal notice of intent to sue Vantage Data Centers and VoltaGrid on July 22. The notice is a required step before filing a citizen lawsuit under the federal Clean Air Act; it does not establish that the companies violated the law.

The projects at 14270 Omicron Drive and 5207 Rogers Road include two natural-gas power plants and 151 backup diesel generators. Together, the dedicated “behind-the-meter” systems, which serve the data centers rather than the regional grid, provide 423 megawatts of primary generating capacity.

The groups contend Vantage and VoltaGrid treated the equipment as separate, minor pollution sources when the interconnected operations should have been evaluated as major sources. In 2024 and 2025, the companies obtained four minor-source authorizations from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality.

According to the legal notice, the facilities have the potential — not necessarily the expectation — to emit approximately 5,600 tons of nitrogen oxides and 323 tons of volatile organic compounds annually. Those pollutants help create ground-level ozone. The groups also estimate potential emissions of 1,190 tons of carbon monoxide and more than 70 tons of formaldehyde, a known human carcinogen.

The allegations carry particular significance because TCEQ classifies Bexar County as a “serious” ozone nonattainment area, meaning it does not meet the federal health standard for ozone.

Major-source permits generally require pollution controls, monitoring and opportunities for public participation before construction. The environmental groups say those safeguards were bypassed.

Vantage said it worked with regulators throughout development, would review the allegations and remains committed to legal compliance and responsible operations. VoltaGrid and TCEQ did not respond to TPR to provide comment, while the EPA declined to comment.

Guests:

title: Need backup power? Automakers want you to look no further than their vehicles in your driveway
description:

So when Kovar, 64, bought a Ford F-150 last fall, his hope was to be better prepared for any new crisis.
“I was interested in trying to find some sort of power backup situation,” he said.

The automaker says its solution is a less expensive way to supply backup power.
text:
Winter Storm Uri, the multiday freeze that slammed Texas in February 2021 and pummeled the state's power grid, has been on Kenneth Kovar's mind ever since. Though the resident of New Braunfels, northeast of San Antonio, didn't lose power at the time, he wasn't able to run his septic tank — it is independent from local systems. He had to fill his toilets with water from his backyard pool.

So when Kovar, 64, bought a Ford F-150 last fall, his hope was to be better prepared for any new crisis.

“I was interested in trying to find some sort of power backup situation,” he said.

Now, Kovar has a setup from Ford that allows drivers of certain F-150 models to plug their vehicle directly into their electric meter to power parts of their home during an outage.

It is the latest example of automakers broadly adapting their electrification technologies to the home energy business, especially as demand on the grid increases and sales of electric vehicles slow. Car companies are looking to leverage their multibillion dollar EV investments to tap into a promising market in vehicle, home and grid technology, both for backup power and for supporting electrical grid resiliency.

“They’re trying to look for other businesses that they might sell into,” said Parth Vaishnav, assistant professor of sustainable systems at the University of Michigan.

Drivers of the F-150 PowerBoost hybrid and F-150 Lightning electric pickup trucks can now plug in a one-foot long adapter to a 240-volt outlet onboard. That adapter — which Ford made with company Global Power Products — makes the vehicle compatible to plug into a longer, separate cable. That cable connects to a transfer switch installed directly on one's electric meter.

Through the adapter and cable series, homeowners can connect their vehicle essentially right to their home’s breaker box. The homeowner simply turns on and off which breaker switches they want for which devices they want powered.

“The way we think about it, especially for customers who already have a compatible vehicle is, you already own the power source, it’s in your driveway,” said Amanda Roraff, Ford's grid and energy services business acceleration lead.

The Lightning might provide power for two to three days, depending on what home devices are being used, and the PowerBoost Hybrid, up to five days on a single tank of gas.

The automaker says its solution is a less expensive way to supply backup power. Conventional, diesel-powered portable generators and full-home standby setups require expensive installation, costing several thousands of dollars. This solution, which also requires professional installation at the meter, starts around $1,100.

The setup only applies to about 200,000 vehicles so far, and it is also exclusively for outages. Ford also offers its Home Integration System for bidirectionality, sending power both from the vehicle to the home and from the home to the vehicle, while also being able to feed the grid.

Over 630,000 U.S. vehicles already have this functionality, estimates say, and automakers are rapidly expanding their available options with the goal of full vehicle-to-grid support in the long run.

South Korean auto brand Kia and Wallbox, an EV charging company, have teamed up so that drivers of eligible compatible vehicles can have home power backup during outages or during periods of high demand, to cut their utility use. They can send power back to the grid.

Tesla’s technology is similar — allowing drivers of equipped vehicles to connect to their home using additional Tesla hardware. The Cybertruck provides full vehicle-to-home capability, where other Tesla models can only connect to and power specific devices or appliances.

General Motors is also in the energy space.

A recent partnership with WeaveGrid, for instance, allows homeowners who drive certain GM EVs — and have the automaker’s home system and a proper grid interconnection — to enroll in some grid reliability utility programs. Once an outage is detected, GM’s vehicle-to-home tech has the capability to disconnect one's home from the grid and start supplying power from their GM EV.

“If you can imagine the future as we go forward, it's having the ability — now that we have this single platform — that allows our customer to experience our system,” said Wade Sheffer, vice president of GM energy, “but also can have the full control of the energy.”

Not only is this business critical amid growing grid demand and increasing power outages, experts say automakers need to pivot with the EV market less active under current U.S. federal policy. Pure EV sales in the U.S. year-over-year are down 23.8%, according to a July Cox Automotive report on the first half of 2026. This demonstrates what an asset that EV and hybrid ownership can be.

The tech is not without challenges.

On the industry side, these systems have to undergo third-party testing to ensure they meet safety standards, and the vehicle and the charger need to be programmed to communicate. It also requires the approval of the utility where the capability is being used. It could take years to get an interconnect agreement.

On the customer side, homeowners need to understand their vehicles' abilities and how to self-manage their system. It also just brings another generator of power into the home mix.

Still, experts see opportunity, especially with interest in EV sales high outside of the U.S.

“We already know during an outage, its impact, providing electricity to the home,” said Scott Samuelsen, engineering professor emeritus at the University of California, Irvine. “This is going to become very, very popular.”

text:
The Trump administration announced Monday that it is exempting power plants that only serve data centers and do not connect to the broader grid from pollution limits that seek to prevent acid rain.

The administration announced new guidance on Monday clarifying that these “islanded” power plants do not have to be part of the Clean Air Act’s Acid Rain Program (ARP).

This program requires power plants to reduce emissions of acid rain precursors sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.

Acid rain can cause environmental damage, including to aquatic wildlife, such as fish. In addition, exposure to sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides can worsen respiratory issues in humans.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said it was taking the action to try to help data centers flourish while also mitigating their impacts on consumer electric bills by incentivizing data centers to bring their own power plants instead of relying on the electricity that’s already on the grid.

“Ensuring that the United States maintains our artificial intelligence dominance is essential to national security and economic prosperity. At the same time, it is equally important that we safeguard our communities from utility price hikes,” EPA Assistant Administrator for Air and Radiation Aaron Szabo said in a statement.

“This guidance will provide an avenue to do both. EPA is proud to further the President’s agenda through commonsense approaches to regulating,” Szabo added.

The announcement comes as the Trump administration is trying to get data centers to build their own power sources to try to blunt the impacts of their high electricity use on consumer electric bills.

This is also not the first time the Trump administration is prioritizing data centers over environmental concerns. Last month, it backed Elon Musk’s xAI in court after the NAACP accused the company of illegal air pollution.

The administration has also previously sought to curtail environmental reviews of data centers and expedite approvals of new chemicals that are expected to be used for them.

The EPA’s new guidance says that because the acid rain program is supposed to apply to electric utilities, power plants that serve data centers should not count because it does not consider them to be utilities.

“The EPA believes that, considering the plain text of these definitions, the ARP does not apply to power generation facilities that are not connected in any way to the larger electricity grid,” the guidance document said.

The EPA said it was issuing the document after states and companies contacted the agency “requesting clarity on certain regulatory provisions in the Acid Rain Program.”

text:
Companies that have been developing wind and solar projects have found their plans scuttled by changes in federal policy under the Trump administration, including changes in tax laws and regulations, but a recent court decision provided them with a little breathing room.

Processing Content

Last month, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia vacated the Internal Revenue Service's Notice 2025-42, which updated the "beginning of construction" rules for wind and solar projects seeking certain clean energy tax credits. The court decision in Oregon Environmental Council v IRS at least temporarily disrupted the push to begin construction on solar and wind projects before July 4, 2026.

Taxpayers can now revert to the earlier guidance under Notice 2013-29 and Notice 2018-59. Both of those notices allow a project to start construction by beginning physical work of significant nature or meeting the 5% safe harbor, regardless of the project type or size. These methodologies have been recognized as the standard for BOC for over a decade, giving some flexibility to projects that initially pivoted away from the safe harbor when faced with the constraints of the 2025 notice.

"Having the court step in and do something is not a big surprise on some level," said Stephen Eckert, practice leader of the national tax office at Plante Moran, a Top 25 Firm based in Southfield, Michigan. "What was different is we don't often see challenges to notices because notices often provide safe harbors or taxpayer-favorable positions. This one was very different in the sense that it was a notice carrying out an executive order to really restrict credits in a particular way."

The rules emerged after the passage last July of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which sharply reduced the tax credits available for renewable energy projects under the earlier Inflation Reduction Act, which passed in 2022 during the Biden administration. The notice came out last fall, Eckert noted, and at the time there were concerns about the phaseout for wind and solar projects pushing up against the beginning of construction date of July 4. Based on the notice, many projects had already pivoted and assumed they would need to pass a so-called "physical work test," requiring a taxpayer to begin physical work of a significant nature to qualify for tax credits. Wind and solar project developers also wouldn't have the benefit of a 5% safe harbor that's typically available as an alternative to the physical work test, requiring taxpayers to pay or incur 5% or more of the total cost of the facility in the year in which construction begins. The court ruling will help developers overcome these hurdles, but Eckert believes they still need to be careful and not take anything for granted.

"What's interesting on this one is just the timing," said Eckert. "Pretty late in the game to try to build the beginning of construction position, the court steps in and the notice is thrown into question. Seemingly you would have potential to apply the 5% safe harbor for relevant wind and solar projects. We've been counseling a little bit of caution as this development occurred for a lot of our projects. If you were planning to meet the physical work test, don't all of a sudden change and think you're just going to meet the 5% safe harbor. Let's continue planning and move forward with the physical work test to satisfy that safe harbor. This may also open a door to then have a fallback or a secondary position to bolster your beginning of construction date by satisfying the 5% safe harbor. In general we've been viewing this as an additional opportunity to further strengthen the beginning of construction position, but I'm not necessarily counting on this being the status quo moving forward."

Companies should continue to move forward under both frameworks when it's feasible and don't assume the 5% safe harbor will remain indefinitely available, Eckert advises clients. He believes taxpayers should proceed with caution and maintain a strategic overview of both current circumstances and potential changes. Most project owners already developed robust BOC strategies in response to Notice 2025-42 before the court ruling. The ultimate resolution won't occur until after the July 4 deadline at this point.

As always with BOC, project owners must maintain comprehensive records of physical work activities, incurred costs and the timing of contract execution and payments, Eckert noted. Such detailed documentation will become crucial should IRS scrutiny arise years down the road.

The decision offers optionality in planning but doesn't ensure certainty. Developers should avoid making any drastic changes unless there's a clear, strategic benefit. If anything, this decision may allow some owners of projects that otherwise had accepted credit noneligibility due to timing constraints to get back into the game. While this situation may be limited, it's worth considering.

Keep a vigilant watch on appeals, new IRS guidance and further court rulings to adjust strategies proactively and adaptively, Eckert cautions. The situation will likely continue to evolve quickly in the weeks and months ahead. Smaller projects get a little bit of breathing room at least.

"This beginning of construction by July 4, 2026 became a relevant matter because the One Big Beautiful Bill started to phase out these credits and gave this elongated period to begin construction and that if you placed it in service in the future that you can claim the credits as long as you begin construction by this date," said Eckert. "If you failed this beginning construction date, as long as you place in service these wind and solar projects by the end of 2027 you still qualify. For smaller-scale wind and solar, you still have the opportunity to complete the project by the end of next year. You have another 18 months, basically, to do that. The challenge is if we're talking utility-scale wind and solar — projects in the tens of millions of dollars, if not more — then the timeline for permitting and construction and sourcing everything to get that done is a bigger lift."

Energy-efficient buildings

Companies working on wind, solar and energy efficiency projects may be able to benefit from doing cost segregation studies after the OBBBA phased out tax breaks like the Section 179D deduction for energy-efficient commercial buildings. Under the OBBBA, the deduction isn't allowed for any property where the construction starts after June 30, 2026.

"There's definitely a higher demand as far as looking at tax rates and interest rates," said Daniel Hurtado, cost segregation leader at Cherry Bekaert, a Top 25 Firm based in Raleigh, North Carolina. "Clients are looking for opportunities to minimize taxable income and increase deductions. There's definitely more of a demand for cost segregation. Also, there were some tax provisions that are sunsetting, like 179D, that are helping drive some renewed interest in cost segregation. If anything, it seems like there's definitely been a higher uptick of interest in the need for cost segregation studies as of recently."

He noted that the Section 179D deduction applies to qualifying improvements to interior lighting, HVAC, hot water systems and the building envelope. The deduction is claimed when the qualifying property is placed in service.

The sunset rule is set for construction projects starting after June 30, 2026. Any project starting post June 2026 will no longer be eligible. For 2025, the maximum deduction is up to $5.81 per square foot when prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements are met.

The OBBBA added a new Section 168(n) to the Internal Revenue Code, allowing a 100% first-year depreciation deduction for Qualified Production Property. The QPP rule replaces the standard 39-year straight-line depreciation for eligible domestic manufacturing, production, refining and agricultural real property placed in service through 2030. Hurtado noted this is the first time certain 39-year building property can be immediately expensed if it meets the QPP rules. It applies to taxpayer buildings used as an integral part of a qualified production activity, manufacturing, chemical production, agricultural production or refining in the U.S.

To be eligible, construction must begin after Jan. 19, 2025, and before Jan. 1, 2029. In addition, the property must be placed in service after July 4, 2025, and before Jan. 1, 2031.

"If it's manufacturing related, then the actual portion of the building that's dedicated to that activity will qualify," said Hurtado. "We're basically going to be taking bonus depreciation for the first time on 39-year property. Bonus depreciation has always been applicable to shorter lived property, but now with this QPP, we're actually going to be having 39-year property that's eligible for bonus appreciation."

That could help incentivize more manufacturing to be done inside the U.S., as well as production activities in the oil refining, agricultural and chemical sectors.

"From our standpoint, it definitely seems like there's been an uptick in the market interest and need for people doing cost segregation studies, as well as tax planning," said Hurtado. "Our tax credits and incentives team focuses on not just cost segregation but also R&D studies as well as New Markets [Tax] Credits. There definitely seems to be a lot of planning discussions for new investments that our team is handling with clients. That's definitely on the positive side to see higher interest in tax planning around capital investments."

text:
By Pedro Barata, Roh Ramirez and Pedro Piris-Cabezas

Just over eighteen months from today, the world’s first truly global carbon market will face a consequential deadline. Airline operators will be required to fulfill their offsetting obligations under the first phase of the International Civil Aviation Organization’s Carbon Offsetting Reduction Scheme for International Aviation.

This deadline has weighed heavily on many of us who have worked hard over the years to make CORSIA a success. CORSIA was designed to achieve carbon-neutral growth in international aviation from 2021-2035. However, as airlines approach the January 31, 2028 deadline to retire Eligible Emissions Units covering 2024-2026 emissions, supply for these units faces tight constraints.

What happens over the course of the next year will define CORSIA’s role, not just to decarbonize the aviation sector, but as a backbone of global carbon markets.

Where are we: CORSIA 2024-2026

This coming October will mark CORSIA’s tenth anniversary. Adopted in October 2016, the flagship United Nations market-based mechanism for international aviation is designed to be implemented in three phases: (1) the pilot phase (2021-2023); (2) Phase 1 (2024-2026); and (3) Phase 2 (2027-2035). The pilot and first phase are voluntary, but in 2027, CORSIA will be mandatory for States with a larger aviation footprint. As of July 2025, 130 States confirmed voluntary participation in CORSIA’s pilot and first phase.

The impact of COVID-19 on the aviation industry significantly reduced emissions in the sector, which meant that CORSIA’s pilot phase did not create offsetting obligations. However, due to CORSIA’s tightened cap and the industry’s quick recovery with record-breaking volumes of passenger traffic in 2025, Phase 1 of CORSIA is expected to generate offsetting requirements of 100-150 million tonnes of CO2, according to ICAO.

To fulfill their offsetting obligations, air carriers can either use CORSIA eligible fuels, including sustainable aviation fuels and lower carbon aviation fuels of fossil origin, or purchase and cancel CORSIA Eligible Emissions Units (EEUs) that meet specific emission unit criteria and can only be issued by eligible offsetting programs. Each EEU represents 1 tonne of CO2 reduction, avoidance or removal outside of the aviation sector. As of today, ICAO has recognized ten emission unit programs that can issue EEUs for Phase 1 covering activities such as: high integrity jurisdictional REDD+, carbon capture and storage, clean cook stoves projects and certain renewable electricity projects, among other activities.

According to ICAO’s own live tracker, there are only around 41 million EEUs verified, issued and labeled as eligible by the programs. Considering an expected demand of between 100-150 million tCO2 for 2024-2026 according to ICAO, this implies that we still need up to four times the current level of eligible EEUs for air carriers to meet their offsetting obligations in time for the first consequential deadline in January 2028 – making this one of the strongest demand signals in global carbon markets today.

As of today, host-country authorization – a critical requirement to avoid double counting and ensuring the integrity of the units – continues to be the main hurdle to a robust EEU supply. Nonetheless, as reported by the Article 6 Implementation Partnership, progress is evident. Fourteen countries have authorization and tracking arrangements in place while an additional eighty-six countries are either considering or in the process to have these in place.

Some potential turbulence and bright developments along the way

Over the last couple of years, new geopolitical shifts, weakened climate momentum and renewed energy insecurity have complicated countries’ efforts to meet CORSIA obligations and sustain focus on long-term climate solutions. Recent volatility in global oil markets has also shifted the aviation industry’s focus away from decarbonization.

Adding another layer of complexity, the EU Commission last week issued its assessment of CORSIA to date and its effectiveness as a tool to reduce climate pollution from aviation within the European Economic Area. CORSIA owes its existence, in part due to the EU’s proposal in 2008 to include all flights arriving and departing from European airports in its EU Emission Trading System (EU ETS). Major backlash from the United States, China, Japan and other countries led to a decision by the EU to “stop the clock” and allow for a global measure (what is now CORSIA) to address international aviation emissions. On July 17, 2026, the European Commission proposed to partially lift that measure for four years for some routes beginning in 2029.

In its environmental integrity assessment of CORSIA, the Commission underscored that ICAO had not strengthened its ambition and that State participation in the global market-based measure still represented less than 70% of international aviation emissions. The Commission also underscored the need to address “hub leakage” to inform its proposal.

The EU Commission is proposing to:

• Expand EU ETS coverage to international aviation covering all routes departing from the EEA and landing within 5,000 kilometers from the largest hub in central Europe (presumably Frankfurt), including flights to hubs in the Middle East and North Africa but effectively excluding flights landing from the United States, Latin America or China.

• Deduct the cost of emissions covered by CORSIA from the newly covered routes in the EU ETS based on a credit price index.

• Expand coverage for all business jet flights that otherwise fell below a minimum emissions threshold.

• Review the EU ETS coverage of international aviation and restrict its application if by July 2032: (1) CORSIA has been strengthened to achieve ICAO’s long-term aspirational goal, towards meeting the Paris Agreement goals; (2) States participating in CORSIA represent more than 70% of international aviation emissions.

In parallel, the EU Commission is reviewing whether to allow the purchase of international carbon credits toward its 2040 climate targets, which could expand the global supply of carbon credits in the coming years and improve the EU’s position in global climate diplomacy. If greenlit, this could create an additional market signal for investors and project developers of offsetting programs. The framework expected later this year will set the environmental integrity and quality bar, government standards and safeguards that will shape the relevant offset supply markets from the start. Though not directly involving CORSIA initially, this will inevitably have an impact – CORSIA offset supply markets will quickly see dramatic improvement around the world as host countries finalize terms and put relevant infrastructure into place, incentivized as sellers to the European buyer.

From a legislative perspective, it is important to recall that the July 17 EU Commission proposal is simply the beginning of a long and unpredictable EU co-decision legislative process that will end up with a Trialogue involving the co-legislators and the Commission sometime in 2027.

Moving forward with a stronger integration of global carbon markets

At this crossroads, and to ensure CORSIA’s success in the near term, it is crucial to support and build capacity for host countries to be able to generate high integrity EEU-generating units. It is crucial that sufficient credit supply is generated in the coming 18 months, and that such supply is indeed leading to not only emission reductions but with adequate safeguards and co-benefits.

In that regard, EDF will continue to support that effort by providing host country support and advice on how to consider and structure their authorization processes, while helping proof of concept carbon credit transactions at large scale in the immediate future. EDF will also continue working toward strengthening CORSIA’s ambition in line with ICAO’s net zero carbon goal by 2050 and expanding its scope to cover all climate impacts, notably from condensation trails and nitrogen oxides, while minimizing public health impacts.

A narrow window and a real opportunity

The tenth anniversary of CORSIA’s adoption arrives alongside its first real test: a supply of eligible emissions units that, as it stands, covers only a fraction of what airlines will need to meet their Phase 1 obligations by January 2028 – not to mentioned larger demand for Phase 2 covering 2027-2035, which ICAO estimates between 880 and 1350 million tons. Closing the supply gap will take sustained, practical work in the countries positioned to generate units, paired with the kind of integrity and safeguards that make those credits trustworthy.

None of this is guaranteed, and the flight path between now and 2028 will have real challenges. But the pieces are visibly moving in the right direction, and the next year offers a rare opportunity to prove that a truly global carbon market can work – for aviation, and as a model for the climate finance architecture the world still needs to build.

John P. Schmitz contributed to this post.

title: Department of Energy declares emergency in Arkansas, 16 other states amid heat wave
description:
(KNWA/KFTA) — The Department of Energy has issued an emergency for 17 states during the intense heat wave currently affecting the country.
The release states that the order will help reduce the possibility of power outages and keep access to electricity stable across the country.
“The previous administration’s energy subtraction policies weakened the grid, leaving Americans more vulnerable during emergency events.
Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we are reversing those failures and using every available tool to ensure Americans have continued access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy to power and cool their homes.” Arkansas was among 17 states named in the emergency order.
The other states are Oklahoma, Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, South Dakota, Texas, Utah and Wyoming.
text:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. (KNWA/KFTA) — The Department of Energy has issued an emergency for 17 states during the intense heat wave currently affecting the country.

The emergency allows the Southwest Power Pool, Inc. to “dispatch specified generation units and to order their operation as needed to maintain reliability,” according to a news release from the DoE.

The release states that the order will help reduce the possibility of power outages and keep access to electricity stable across the country.

“The Trump Administration is tapping into an abundant supply of unused backup generation to maintain affordable, reliable, and secure power for hardworking American families and businesses,” U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in a release. “The previous administration’s energy subtraction policies weakened the grid, leaving Americans more vulnerable during emergency events. Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we are reversing those failures and using every available tool to ensure Americans have continued access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy to power and cool their homes.”

Arkansas was among 17 states named in the emergency order.

The other states are Oklahoma, Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, South Dakota, Texas, Utah and Wyoming.

All of the SPP operations will be required to follow requirements to mitigate environmental impacts.

The order will expire on August 3.

text:
LANDER, Wyo. — Rocky Mountain Farmers Union (RMFU) is proud to announce that President Chad Franke has been appointed to serve on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Farm, Ranch, and Rural Communities Committee (FRRCC).

The committee brings together agricultural leaders from across the country to provide the EPA with recommendations and guidance on environmental issues and policies that affect farmers, ranchers, and rural communities.

Franke’s appointment ensures that the perspectives of farmers and ranchers in the West are represented as the committee considers issues impacting agriculture nationwide. Producers across the Rocky Mountain region face unique challenges, including water scarcity, prolonged drought, wildfire risk, and public land management. RMFU believes having a leader with firsthand experience navigating these realities will help advance practical, producer-driven solutions that recognize the needs of rural communities.

“President Franke’s appointment to the Farm, Ranch, and Rural Communities Committee is a testament to the leadership, practical knowledge, and commitment he brings to advancing family agriculture,” said Tyler Garrett, RMFU Chief Executive Officer. “Chad has been a steadfast advocate for policies that strengthen rural communities and ensure family farmers and ranchers have a voice in the decisions that affect their livelihoods. His experience as a farmer, engineer, and Farmers Union leader gives him a unique perspective on the opportunities and challenges facing agriculture today. We are confident his collaborative approach and commitment to practical solutions will make him a valuable contributor to the committee and help ensure family agriculture is well represented at the national level.”

“I appreciate the opportunity to serve on this committee and help bring the voices of western farmers and ranchers to the table,” Franke said. “The best policies are developed when the people who live and work on the land have a seat in the conversation. I look forward to working with fellow committee members to identify practical solutions that protect our natural resources while supporting the producers and rural communities that depend on them.”

The EPA established the FRRCC in 2007 to provide policy advice, information, and recommendations to the EPA Administrator on environmental issues affecting agriculture and rural America. Franke will serve a two-year term on the committee.

Since water heating accounts for nearly 19% of residential energy consumption, widespread adoption of HPWHs can significantly reduce energy usage and greenhouse gas emissions .

text:
Roughly 40 people gathered at the Hackberry Community Center last week, for a public hearing on a planned carbon dioxide sequestration project in the area. If approved, the planned carbon sequestration injection well project would be the third of its kind in the state, and the second in Cameron Parish.

The permit would allow Lake Charles-based Gulf Coast Sequestration to inject and sequester up to 19 million metric tons of CO2 into two wells, 8,900 to 10,500 feet below ground level, over a 30-year period.

Public comments included two GCS company representatives in support of the permit application, five Southwest Louisiana residents in favor of the project, and nine against it.

Those in favor of granting the permit touted economic growth and job creation, as well as rigorous safety and monitoring protocols.

But project opponents worried about potential CO2 leaks and water contamination, delayed emergency response times, and proximity to nearby salt domes used for natural gas storage. They also questioned the transparency of the project.

Company representatives wrote the construction phase of the project would generate 300 temporary jobs, “with a workforce comprising approximately 20% local residents, 70% commuters, and 10% individuals temporarily relocating to the area,” according to documents filed with the Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy. Once in operation, the project would employ seven full-time positions.

“Through permanent sequestration, we can reduce the carbon dioxide output into the air from these critical local industries,” GCS Head of External Affairs Ryan Furby said at the hearing. “We do this by safely storing a deep underground, where it is absorbed permanently into deep rock reservoirs.”

“The service location of the two wells we’re discussing tonight are carefully, thoughtfully, and intentionally located on remote, largely uninhabitable private land that is generally used for ranching,” Furby said.

Project documents indicate “CO2 will be sourced from undisclosed strategic partners in the Lake Charles Industrial Corridor,” a finding Cameron Parish Police Jury Vice President Magnus “Sonny” McGee took issue with.

“The pipeline route is not clear. It may be out of our jurisdiction, but it will affect people wherever it is,” McGee said, and added that it is not reasonable to grant a permit for a well without knowing where it will source the CO2 to inject, or what percentage of impurities will be in it, or the make up of those impurities.

The injections will contain at least 97% CO2 and 3% of other gases and trace elements including methane, hydrogen sulfide and trace amounts of mercury, according to project records.

Hydrogen sulfide is a toxic colorless gas, and prolonged exposure can result in a noticeable odor at the lowest levels, but at higher exposure can cause nausea, headaches, drowsiness and instant death at the highest.

“You ask us to give consent without knowing,” the police juror said.

The Chicot Aquifer is the closest water supply to the project. It has a maximum depth of 1,100 feet below sea level and is the most important aquifer in Louisiana, spanning over 9,000 square miles and supplying 400 million gallons of water per day to 15 parishes.

Gulf Coast Sequestration founder and executive chairman Gray Stream tried to assuage concerns by pointing to his own local ties.

“This is our property, it’s our land. We live here. I raised my kids here, they’re born here, me too. And that’s our whole culture,” Stream said. “This isn’t some kind of evil mega corporation from far away.”

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency typically regulates Class VI wells, but it handed over primacy to Louisiana in early 2024.

After vocal pressure from residents and lawmakers, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry issued an executive order officially pausing new Class VI injection well permit applications after October 2025. But the proposed project is exempt from this moratorium, having been placed on a priority list by Landry in his executive order.

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) issued an emergency order Sunday to keep Americans across 17 states powered as hot weather conditions continue.

What we know:

The order directs Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) to dispatch generator units to operate as a last resort as needed to maintain electric service in the SPP East and West Balancing Authority Areas (BAAs) in the following 17 states:

Texas

Louisiana

Arkansas

Missouri

Iowa

North Dakota

South Dakota

Nebraska

Oklahoma

Kansas

Colorado

Wyoming

Montana

New Mexico

Arizona

Minnesota

Utah

Dig deeper:

The DOE says the order was issued after a request from SPP and directs SPP to dispatch specified generation units and to order their operation as needed to maintain reliability as a last resort before declaring an Energy Emergency Alert 3 (EEA 3), one of the final steps before rolling outages are implemented.

DOE says they estimate there are more than 35 gigawatts (GW) of unused backup generation remaining available nationwide.

What they're saying:

"The Trump Administration is tapping into an abundant supply of unused backup generation to maintain affordable, reliable, and secure power for hardworking American families and businesses," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright in a release.

Big picture view:

The Southwest Power Poll (SPP) is a Regional Transmission Organization headquartered in Little Rock, Arkansas and mandated by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). SPP ensures there are reliable power supplies and manages the electic transmission infrastructure across a multistate territory.

Earlier this year, SPP expanded its territory into the Western Interconnection, integrating utilities across seven states including parts of Arizona, Colorado, and Utah.

text:
LFE, industrial intelligence and CE

A new wave of technological innovation is reshaping China’s economic and industrial landscape. Digital technologies, exemplified by big data, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and blockchain, are accelerating innovation, driving industrial transformation, and enabling the transformation of the economic structure42. Industrial robots, as an integrated system encompassing multiple cutting-edge digital technologies, not only reflect the level of industrial intelligence through their application but also exert a positive influence on enhancing production efficiency, optimizing production processes, and improving operational management in enterprises. However, due to insufficient funds, technical limitations, and other factors, many enterprises in China struggle to achieve intelligent upgrading. Local governments’ LFE can play a crucial role in promoting the widespread adoption of industrial robots in production, thereby leveraging their technological effects to reduce CE. Specifically, first, governments’ LFE contribute to enhancing workforce health, knowledge, and skill levels, fostering human capital effects to meet enterprises’ demand for high-quality labor in intelligent production26,27,43,44. This, incentivizes enterprises to invest in and adopt industrial robots, accelerating the intelligent transformation of urban industries. Second, the rise in labor costs driven by LFE accelerates enterprises’ “replacing humans with machines” process45,46,47. LFE allocated to raising minimum wages and perfecting social security systems improves worker welfare while increasing employment costs for enterprises, thereby motivating them to substitute labor with capital factors48. To maintain competitiveness, enterprises prefer investing in intelligent and automated equipment to reduce long-term labor costs. Finally, local governments’ efforts to optimize basic public services have significantly improved the urban business environment49. For local enterprises, this boosts business confidence and increases long-term investment in industrial robot R&D and application50, driving upgrades in industrial robot technology and intelligent production systems. Meanwhile, it is conducive to attracting more external robotics companies and related supporting enterprises into the city51, further elevating the local industrial intelligence level.

At present, the level of industrial intelligence has become a key indicator of a city’s core competitiveness, while the extent to which local enterprises apply industrial robots in their production processes represents the micro-level manifestation of a city’s industrial intelligence. The application of industrial robots profoundly transforms enterprise production models, enabling the efficient allocation of production factors and resources, thereby enhancing production efficiency while reducing resource consumption, ultimately promoting clean production practices52. The root cause of industrial intelligence driving CER lies in green technological progress. On the one hand, industrial robots serve as application carriers for multiple cutting-edge digital technologies, inherently representing the direction of technological advancement while possessing green attributes. On the other hand, the deployment of industrial robots provides superior hardware conditions for innovative activities by enterprise R&D personnel. By leveraging advanced technologies such as intelligent management and smart algorithms, this facilitates breakthroughs in green technologies, extends enterprises’ technological development boundaries in terms of efficiency improvement and carbon emission reduction, and assists enterprises in achieving efficient green technological innovation53,54. Through the application of automation systems with high intelligence and autonomy, as well as the green and clean transformation of traditional production models, industrial intelligence can effectively alleviate issues such as energy waste, redundant investment, or unreasonable investment structures, thereby improving energy efficiency and reducing CE in the production process55.

LFE, market integration and CE

For a long time, China’s rigid administrative divisions have led to the segmentation of factor markets, resulting in losses in factor allocation efficiency. However, inter-regional free flow of factors and resource reallocation driven by local government LFE can effectively alleviate market segmentation and promote market integration. The “voting by foot” theory, proposed by Tiebout56, elucidates the motivation behind labor mobility: when migration is unrestricted, laborers tend to settle in regions that offer higher-quality public services. Consequently, increasing LFE and optimizing the provision of basic public services within local jurisdictions serve as crucial factors in attracting labor inflows. According to enterprise growth and new economic geography theories, local government improvements of people’s livelihoods can promote human capital accumulation, the optimization of the business environment, and enhanced enterprise production performance within the region. This, in turn, increases the rate of return on capital, thereby attracting capital inflows from other areas57. Evidently, the provision of livelihood public services also represents a potential pathway for driving long-term, sustainable capital flows58. Currently, the way local governments compete for production factors has transitioned from low-level, extensive competition primarily based on tax breaks to high-level competition that integrates fiscal incentives, infrastructure development, public services, and other measures59. While fiscal subsidies and tax incentives largely affect only one parameter within a firm’s profit function, government LFE profoundly influences local quality of life and welfare levels through education, healthcare, and other sectors. This approach may prove more effective in attracting high-caliber talent and high-quality capital inflows24. The inflow of factors driven by increased LFE not only stimulates local economic growth but also generates more tax revenue for local governments, which in turn incentivizes governments to further expand LFE, thereby forming a virtuous cycle mechanism.

Regarding the impact of market integration on CE. First, as market integration continues to advance, factor markets are gradually evolving from segmentation to unification and playing a decisive role in resource allocation. The free flow of factors under market integration is conducive to promoting industrial cooperation and division of labor among regions, decreasing the degree of industrial homogeneity, and enhancing the efficient allocation of production factors and corporate productivity. The industrial division of labor contributes to the formation of economies of scale, effectively reducing resource waste in production processes, increasing resource utilization rates, and minimizing unnecessary CE caused by homogeneous production. Secondly, high-quality talent, superior capital, and advanced technology are crucial elements for urban transformation. Market integration lays a solid market foundation for cities to attract talent, capital, and other factors and form high-quality factor agglomeration. Notably, under market integration, the positive spillover effects of technological innovation are more pronounced, facilitating coordinated carbon emission reduction efforts across regions60. Finally, market integration is expected to strengthen the market competition effect. Since some high-polluting, high-energy-consuming, and low-efficiency enterprises lack core competitiveness in market competition, they struggle to sustain operations under the dual pressures of technological backwardness and insufficient funding, ultimately being forced to exit the market. This drives more production factors concentrating on high-efficiency enterprises, thereby enhancing regional energy utilization rates and productivity levels while also achieving regional CER61,62. Thus, according to the above analysis, this paper proposes the following hypotheses:

H1. LFE can promote urban CER to address climate change.

H2. LFE drives industrial intelligence transformation by promoting the widespread adoption of industrial robots, thereby achieving urban CER.

H3. LFE mainly advances market integration by facilitating the flow and reallocation of factors, thereby reducing urban CE.

The Impact of LFE on CE under regional competition

In China’s unique political evaluation system, GDP serves as the key performance criterion for assessing the achievements of local officials, which significantly influences their prospects for political advancement. The promotion tournament theory reveals that economic competition among local governments exerts profound influence on fiscal expenditure structures, infrastructure development, and industrial growth within their jurisdictions. The specific pathways through which local government competition affects the carbon reduction effectiveness of the LFE are as follows:

On the one hand, local government competition exerts a crowding-out effect on LFE. Fiscal expenditures serve as the primary means for local officials to participate in the GDP tournament. Under the dual pressures of economic growth and political advancement, competition among local governments leads to irrational and short-sighted fiscal spending behavior, thereby distorting the structure of fiscal expenditures63. Local governments, in pursuit of greater economic benefits, tend to concentrate fiscal expenditure on productive sectors. Under a fiscal expenditure pattern characterized by “prioritizing production over livelihood”, excessive and repetitive investment generate numerous negative consequences, including resource waste, increased pollution emissions, low fiscal expenditure efficiency, and declines in livelihood welfare64. Specifically, local governments’ excessive investment in infrastructure, such as energy, transportation, and other sectors, exhibits a carbon lock-in effect. The construction process of these facilities is characterized by high energy consumption and emissions, and once completed, they typically serve existing high-carbon industrial systems. This locks cities’ energy consumption structures and industrial production models onto high-carbon pathways. Simultaneously, owing to the crowding-out of LFE, human capital accumulation remains insufficient, failing to provide adequate support for industrial upgrading. Consequently, local economic development becomes locked into capital-intensive yet relatively low-technology manufacturing paths, making industrial restructuring difficult and keeping CE at persistently high levels.

On the other hand, there is the impact of economic competition among local governments on enterprises. Local governments typically employ fiscal incentives and infrastructure improvements as supportive measures to attract external enterprises to invest and establish operations65,66,67. However, some regions, striving for rapid economic growth in the short term, may exhibit regulatory laxity and policy abuse. Local governments may tacitly approve low-end manufacturing enterprises to package themselves as high-tech enterprises to secure fiscal subsidies68. While this may temporarily attract more external enterprises and stimulate local economic development, it exacerbates the disorderly agglomeration of low-end manufacturing industries, hinders industrial structure upgrading and productivity improvements, and leads to higher CE. For local enterprises, local governments may adopt fiscal measures to protect them and prevent their exit from the local market, aiming to safeguard the local tax base and increase employment rates. This enables low-productivity enterprises and even those on the verge of bankruptcy to continue to survive69,70. Such protective measures may also dampen local enterprises’ willingness to compete in the market, inhibit their drive for technological innovation and transformation, and hinder further productivity gains and emission reduction.

The Impact of LFE on CE under regional inequality

Since the reform and opening-up, China’s economy has undergone rapid development, and government fiscal expenditures have continued to expand. As a result, the basic public service system is becoming increasingly robust, the level of equalization is constantly improving, and the capacity to ensure service provision is being comprehensively enhanced. People’s demands for basic public services are also gradually transforming from “having the opportunity to enjoy” to “enjoying more, fairer, and higher-quality services”71. The provision of basic public services primarily relies on local LFE. However, due to the persistent issues of unbalanced and inadequate regional development in China, significant disparities still exist in the fiscal revenue and expenditure capacities of different regions, resulting in a notable degree of inequality in LFE72. Inequality in LFE can exacerbate social inequality and widen the wealth gap, thereby constraining the coordinated and high-quality development of the regional economy, and ultimately hindering China’s progress toward common prosperity. Given this, this paper argues that the CER effectiveness of LFE is negatively impacted by its degree of inequality. The primary reason is that the inequality of LFE exacerbates the siphoning effect of large cities on surrounding cities. As mentioned earlier, LFE can promote the flow and reallocation of factor resources, advancing market integration. However, due to regional inequality, central cities, large cities, and relatively economically developed cities can attract more elements and resources by increasing LFE and optimizing basic public services, thereby creating a siphoning effect on surrounding cities. Consequently, non-central cities, medium-sized and small cities, and relatively economically underdeveloped cities experience limited returns on their fiscal expenditures. This implies that even if these cities increase LFE and optimize public services, their ability to attract high-quality talent and capital remains constrained in the short term due to endowment differences.

Furthermore, some detailed implications of LFE inequality may include: First, when selecting locations, enterprises consider the level of public services for people’s livelihood. In cities with higher LFE, enterprises face stricter environmental standards and higher compliance costs, but they also gain access to more green technology support and subsidies, which contribute to promoting CER. Conversely, in cities with lower LFE, some high-pollution, high-energy-consumption enterprises may relocate to avoid environmental costs, thereby turning these cities into areas with high CE levels. Due to significant deficiencies in green technology R&D subsidies and attracting high-quality talent in cities with lower LFE, coupled with the impact of labor outflow, human capital cannot accumulate effectively. This ultimately leads to insufficient technological innovation motivation among polluting enterprises, making it difficult for them to achieve a clean production transformation in the short term. Thus, expenditure inequality distorts enterprise location choices, causing CE to “leak” from high-spending to low-spending cities, thereby weakening overall carbon emission reduction effectiveness. Second, interregional flows of knowledge and technology are impeded, which is not conducive to innovation sharing and technological progress73. Cities with higher LFE tend to possess superior institutional environments. This provides a solid foundation for the agglomeration of high-tech enterprises and other innovation factors, thereby promoting the construction of science and technology innovation hubs. Under the influence of LFE inequality, innovation activities are primarily concentrated in high-spending cities, while knowledge spillovers and technology diffusion to low-spending cities remain limited, exacerbating the technological divide between cities. Consequently, in low-spending cities, production technology levels remain relatively backward. Combined with the lack of green technology, R&D subsidies and high-quality talent, this makes it difficult to effectively reduce CE.

Accordingly, based on the above analysis, the following hypothesis is proposed:

H4. Local government competition and LFE inequality have negative constraint effects, which can weaken the CER effect of LFE.

Figure 1 illustrates the complete process by which LFE influences urban CE.

Analysis of the current situation

The expansion of local government LFE can significantly improve the provision of basic public services in China and strongly guarantee people’s basic rights to enjoy social resources such as education, medical care, social security, and scientific and technological services. Figure 2 illustrates the spatial and temporal distribution characteristics of LFE from 2008 to 2020, focusing on both the growth of the LFE scale and changes in LFE structure. In terms of changes in expenditure scale, the level of LFE during the sample period has increased substantially. In 2008, most cities in China were still at a relatively low level of LFE. Except for the four municipalities directly under the central government, only a few regional central cities reached medium or higher expenditure levels, such as Guangzhou, Wuhan, Chengdu, Hangzhou, and Shenyang. Additionally, the overall expenditure level across the country exhibited an “east high, west low” distribution pattern. By 2020, with the sustained economic growth, the LFE levels in all regions of the country had increased markedly, but the “higher in the east and lower in the west” distribution pattern remained unchanged. From the perspective of changes in the expenditure structure, the proportion of LFE in total fiscal expenditure has also increased to a certain extent. This indicates that since 2008, local governments have gradually increased their emphasis on the provision of public goods such as education, medical care, and social security. However, due to the pressure of economic growth and political promotion, local government officials have been unable to devote more energy to improving livelihood welfare, resulting in a relatively slow increase in the proportion of LFE.

Benchmark regression analysis

Table 1 reports the benchmark regression results examining the impact of LFE on CE. In columns (1) and (2), the coefficients for LFE are –0.15 and –0.188, respectively, and both are statistically significant at the 1% level. This indicates that regardless of whether control variables are included, LFE significantly reduces urban CE. For every one percentage point increase in LFE, urban CE decreases by an average of 0.188%. Thus, the direct impact of LFE on urban CE is confirmed, preliminarily validating H1. This conclusion provides clear, targeted evidence for local governments to increase LFE, optimize public service provision, and steadily promote CER, thereby facilitating urban low-carbon transformation and contributing to the achievement of the “dual carbon” goal, and responding to global climate change. Additionally, considering the potential lag effect of LFE on CE, we introduce one-period and two-period lags of LFE. As shown in the regression results of columns (3) and (4), the coefficients of lagged LFE are both significantly negative, indicating that LFE exerts a long-term influence on CE. Finally, this study conducts regression analyses on various components of LFE. The results indicate that the coefficients for EDU, MED, SEC, and SCI are –0.167, –0.051, –0.028, and –0.043, respectively, all of which are statistically significant and negative. This reaffirms the CER effect of LFE and enhances the robustness of the baseline findings.

Endogeneity discussion

The benchmark regression in this study may have potential endogeneity issues stemming from omitted variables, reverse causality, and other factors. To test for endogeneity in the core explanatory variable LFE, we conduct a Hausman test. The results strongly reject the null hypothesis that LFE is exogenous (p < 0.01). Therefore, this paper employs a two-stage least squares (2SLS) regression using instrumental variables to address endogeneity concerns. Here, two instrumental variables are selected. First, drawing on the instrumental variable construction approach of Fisman and Svensson74, the average of LFE across all other cities in the province (excluding this one city) lagged by two periods is adopted as an instrumental variable (IV_live). Generally, cities within the same province exhibit strategic interactions regarding LFE, thus satisfying the correlation assumption. Simultaneously, the CE of a given city is largely unaffected by the LFE of other cities within its province, and the two-period lagged instrument variable is uncorrelated with the current error term, thereby satisfying the exogeneity assumption. Second, following the methodology of Munshi75, we construct an additional instrumental variable using the one-period lagged number of annual extreme precipitation days (IV_erd). This variable is calculated based on the daily city-level precipitation data and the classification standard for rainstorms (daily precipitation exceeding 50 mm). Flooding disasters triggered by extreme precipitation compel local governments to rapidly increase short-term fiscal expenditures on disaster relief and water conservancy. After the disaster response concludes, the corresponding LFE may be elevated to safeguard public welfare. Consequently, the one-period lagged extreme precipitation satisfies the relevance assumption. As a natural phenomenon, extreme precipitation is obviously random and exogenous. The one-period lagged extreme precipitation days cannot directly influence contemporaneous CE and are fundamentally uncorrelated with the current-period error term, thereby strictly guaranteeing the exogeneity of the instrumental variable.

Columns (1) and (2) of Table 2 report the results of the instrumental variable regression. The Kleibergen-Paap rk LM statistics and Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F statistics are 268.229 and 155.436, respectively, passing the under-identification test and weak instrument test. The Hansen J statistic for the over-identification test is 1.084, with a corresponding p value of 0.298, which is greater than 0.1, indicating that all instrumental variables are exogenous. After considering the potential endogeneity between LFE and urban CE, the second-stage regression results demonstrate that the coefficient of LFE on urban CE remains significantly negative, indicating that the conclusions of the benchmark regression are not affected by endogeneity issues, and H1 is further supported. In addition, to ensure the robustness of the endogeneity analysis, this study also employs the System GMM method for estimation. Column (3) reports the estimation results, where the coefficient of the core explanatory variable LFE remains significantly negative at the 1% level, consistent with the instrumental variable regression results.

Robustness test

This paper conducts robustness tests across the following five dimensions:

First, replace the core explanatory variable. The core explanatory variable is replaced with the degree of local government’s preference for LFE (FES), calculated as the proportion of LFE to the total fiscal expenditure. The results in column (1) of Table 3 indicate that a higher degree of local government preference for LFE strengthens its inhibitory effect on CE.

Second, we replace the explained variable. The explained variable is replaced with CE intensity (CI), measured as the ratio of total CE in prefecture-level cities to GDP. The lower the value of this indicator, the less CE is generated per unit of GDP. According to the regression results in column (2), the coefficient of LFE remains significantly negative, indicating a significant reduction in urban CE intensity.

Third, we adjust the sample scope. The 2020 COVID-19 pandemic had a substantial shock on both China and the global economy, resulting in short-term economic stagnation. Given the atypical nature of the 2020 data, which could introduce bias into the full-sample estimation, this paper excludes data from that year in the regression analysis. The regression results in column (3) remain consistent with those of the full sample.

Fourth, we apply winsorization. To avoid the impact of outliers in the sample data on the regression results, this paper conducts a 1% winsorization treatment on both the upper and lower bounds of all continuous variables and re-estimates the model. The regression results, presented in column (4), remain consistent with the benchmark findings.

Finally, we control for policy effects. To accurately identify the causal relationship between LFE and CE, it is necessary to control for the interference of related emission reduction policies. Therefore, this study simultaneously incorporates the pilot policy of low-carbon city (LC), the pilot policy of carbon emission trading (CET), and the national comprehensive demonstration city of energy saving and emission reduction fiscal policy (GF) into the benchmark regression equation to examine whether the implementation of these policies interferes with the core findings of this study. Column (5) regression results indicate that after accounting for policy interference, the low-carbon effect of LFE remains statistically robust.

The above series of robustness tests further validate H1.

Mechanism test

According to the theoretical analysis in the preceding section, this paper further examines the mechanism through which LFE affects CE, focusing primarily on the dimensions of industrial intelligence and market integration.

Table 4 columns (1)–(3) report the results of mechanisms test examining how LFE influences urban CE by promoting industrial intelligence. In column (1), we use the penetration rate of industrial robots as an indicator to measure the level of industrial intelligence and examine its underlying mechanism. The results reveal that LFE significantly increases industrial robot penetration at the 1% statistical level, thereby promoting the intelligent transformation of urban industry, which supports the industrial intelligence influence mechanism. The human capital enhancement and business environment optimization driven by LFE facilitates the adoption of industrial robots in enterprise production, thereby promoting local industrial intelligent transformation. As an amalgamation of numerous transformative frontier technologies, industrial robots profoundly reshape enterprise production models, simultaneously enhancing productivity, improving resource efficiency, optimizing production processes, and reducing CE.

Furthermore, this paper posits that the green technology effect induced by industrial intelligence is the intrinsic reason through which it facilitates urban CER. Therefore, a more detailed analysis of the industrial intelligence impact mechanism is warranted. This paper integrates green technological progress into the analytical framework, measured through two indicators: green technological innovation capacity and energy efficiency. Column (2) presents the results of the mechanism test for green technological innovation capacity. We find that LFE accelerates the widespread adoption of industrial robots, providing enterprises with superior hardware foundations and intelligent technological support for innovation. This facilitates the enhancement of local enterprises’ capacity for green technological innovation. Thus, the mechanism of green technological innovation capacity is validated. Column (3) reports the results of the mechanism test for energy efficiency. As shown, the coefficient for LFE is significantly positive, indicating that it promotes energy efficiency improvement. This implies that the intelligent transformation driven by industrial robot adoption profoundly reshapes the entire production process, achieving a win-win outcome of energy savings and productivity gains. Such findings validate the existence of the energy efficiency impact mechanism.

The above test results clarify the process of LFE affecting urban CE through the path of industrial intelligence, confirming the role of industrial intelligent transformation and its green technology impact in reducing CE, thereby validating H2.

Columns (4) and (5) of Table 4 report the results of the mechanism analysis for market integration. In column (4), LFE significantly reduces labor market segmentation among cities nationwide and promotes labor market integration. This implies that the cross-regional labor mobility facilitated by LFE, particularly the movement of highly qualified and skilled talent, contributes to the optimal allocation of labor resources and the upgrading of human capital. Column (5) shows that LFE significantly reduces capital market segmentation among different regions, promoting capital market integration. Improvements in urban livelihoods exert a positive influence on attracting high-quality capital inflows, which not only bring new funds to local areas but also often introduce new technologies. Overall, the optimization of public services brought about by LFE can stimulate the free flow of production factors, reduce barriers between regions to a certain extent, and thereby advance the process of market integration and the construction of a unified national market. Under the process of factor market integration, the more efficient allocation of labor and capital facilitates the dissemination and exchange of cutting-edge theoretical knowledge and advanced technologies across regions, thereby establishing a knowledge-sharing mechanism, amplifying technology spillover effects, and contributing to urban CER.

The above test results delineate the process through which LFE influences urban CE by facilitating factor mobility and mitigating market segmentation, confirming the positive role of market integration in driving urban CER. H3 is verified.

Additionally, it should be noted that the potential lagged effects of LFE on industrial intelligence and market integration may compromise the robustness of the mechanism test results. Therefore, we include the one-period-lagged LFE in the regression analysis. The results reveal that the coefficient of L.LFE aligns strongly with the mechanism test findings, reaffirming H2 and H3.
