text:
President Trump ran on a pledge to bring down energy costs, but a year and a half into his second term, prices of both gasoline and electricity are rising.

While he was on the campaign trail, Trump promised to cut power prices by 50 percent.

“Under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least,” he said at a rally.

“We intend to slash prices by half within 12 months, at a maximum 18 months,” he added.

However, average household electricity prices for the first five months of 2026 were about 12 percent higher than the same period in 2024, significantly outpacing inflation.

While gasoline fluctuated during the Biden administration, prices are now about 60 cents higher than they were at this time in 2024, averaging $4.11 per gallon on Friday, according to AAA.

Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, said high energy prices “push up” the cost of living for ordinary Americans.

“They have higher costs of gasoline to run their car. Food costs will increase on the margin because trucks need to deliver groceries. If you use heating oil to heat your home, the cost will be higher,” Wolfe said.

He estimated that if oil remained at $100 per barrel for a year, it could cost families about $800 more a year on gasoline alone.

The high gas prices are a result of the U.S.-Iran war in the Middle East. Turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping lane, and more recently the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait as well, have sent prices soaring.

“On heating oil and gasoline, it’s a direct result of the war. It’s pushing up prices and creating this instability in the market,” Wolfe said.

Asked about the prices, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers accused Iran of breaking a ceasefire with the U.S.

Rogers said that as the U.S. takes down Iran’s ability to attack commercial ships and disrupt trade through the state of Hormuz, “oil and gas prices will plummet back to pre-conflict levels.”

“President Trump remains committed to unleashing American energy dominance, cutting costs, and putting more money back in the pockets of hardworking American families,” she said.

Meanwhile, the electricity price picture is more complicated.

Thomas Rowlands-Rees, head of Global Power Markets Analysis at BloombergNEF, said that prices are going up because “we’re getting to a point where the bill is coming” for grid upgrades, and that it’s not necessarily the fault of any particular administration.

“The government doesn’t have access to that many ‘sticks’ that it can apply to the utility industry, because so much of the policy power there is at the state level,” he said, adding that federal electricity policy has impact on a “timescale of years and decades.”

Rowlands-Rees said that he doesn’t think that any administration would have been able to cut the price in half in 18 months.

“I don’t think it was something that the government could have achieved, even if they made all the right policy choices, because those policy choices wouldn’t have an impact on such a short timescale,” he said.

He added that if anything, the Trump administration’s policies may actually raise prices in the long-term, including its desire to expand exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG), which could increase demand for the fuel.

“The government has been very favorable to encourage expansion of energy extraction in the U.S., which would be a downward pressure, but on the other hand, they’ve also been very bullish on exports of LNG,” he said. “Our current analysis suggests that the U.S.’s ability to export is going to grow faster than the U.S.’s ability to expand supply, so that means there’s going to be potentially in the next few years upward pressure on natural gas prices — and we’re talking about maybe two or three years from now.”

Wolfe, meanwhile, also dinged the administration for the hurdles it has set up for renewable energy.

“It’s not the president’s fault that electricity prices are rising faster than inflation. They’ve been rising faster than inflation for several years,” he said, but he added that “clean energy provides stable pricing.”

The high energy prices could spell trouble for Republicans in the midterm elections.

“It’s a problem for any incumbent,” said GOP strategist Keith Naughton.

“Anything that’s raising prices is going to be a challenge for whoever’s in office,” added Naughton, who also contributes opinion pieces to The Hill.

name: EPA
title: How weakening environmental protections affects communities worldwide | IQAir USA
authors: IQAir Staff Writers, IQAir Staff Writers https:, www.iqair.com
description:
Weakened protections impact health Air pollution already contributes to more than 7 million premature deaths worldwide every year, according to the World Health Organization, making pollution the largest single environmental health risk on the planet (9).
Air pollution’s burden falls unevenly Weakened environmental protections rarely harm everyone equally.
Ecosystems under mounting pressure The ecological toll of weakened protections is playing out across some of the planet's most iconic landscapes.
Stay informed about local and national policy changes that affect environmental protections.
The takeaway Weakening environmental protections is a human issue, which carries immediate consequences for human health and long-term consequences for ecosystem.
text:
Across some of the world's most developed democracies, the United States, the European Union, Australia, and New Zealand governments are rolling back the rules that were enacted to protect public health, stabilize economies, and preserve ecosystems.

These are not isolated national stories. They are connected chapters in a global pattern, one in which industry lobbying, short-term economic pressure, and political expediency are chipping away at decades of environmental progress. And the consequences rarely stay within borders. Polluted air drifts across continents, weakened trade rules ripple through global supply chains, and the erosion of one country's protections can undercut the credibility of international agreements everywhere else.

Where protections are rolling back

In the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency has pursued what its own administrator called the "single largest deregulatory action" in the agency's history.

In February 2026, the EPA finalized a rule eliminating the 2009 Endangerment Finding, the scientific determination that greenhouse gases threaten public health, effectively rescinding the legal foundation for federal emissions standards on cars, trucks, and power plants (1)(2). The agency has also granted coal-fired power plants exemptions from mercury and air toxics standards and repealed a 2024 rule that would have cut emissions of toxic air pollutants from petrochemical plants (3).

The European Union has taken a subtler but no less consequential path. Since 2025, the European Commission has introduced ten "omnibus" packages, bundling changes that weaken corporate sustainability reporting, due diligence, and permitting requirements under the banner of "simplification" (4). Investigations by watchdog groups found that roughly 90% of meetings shaping these packages involved business interests, with heavy industry successfully pushing to delay the EU's carbon border tax, soften vehicle emissions rules, and fast-track permits for polluting infrastructure (5)(6).

New Zealand, a nation long associated with strong conservation records, is also shifting course. New Zealand's coalition government has moved to weaken its National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity and freshwater protections, making it easier to approve mining and quarrying in ecologically sensitive areas (7).

In Brazil, home to the majority of the Amazon rainforest, a new "devastation bill" took effect in February 2026, introducing a self-licensing system that lets developers sign off on their own environmental impact assessments for many projects (8).

Each of these countries built its climate and conservation frameworks over generations. Undoing them, even partially, is proving to have cross-border consequences that fall hardest on the communities least equipped to withstand them.

Weakened protections impact health

Air pollution already contributes to more than 7 million premature deaths worldwide every year, according to the World Health Organization, making pollution the largest single environmental health risk on the planet (9). Weakened protections threaten to push that number higher, and the clearest evidence is emerging in the communities living closest to industrial pollution.

In Louisiana's "Cancer Alley," an 85-mile industrial corridor along the Mississippi River, researchers from Johns Hopkins University found in 2025 that cancer risks from airborne toxins were up to 11 times higher than official EPA estimates, largely because the agency's models rely on companies self-reporting their own emissions (10)(11). Just months earlier, the Trump administration had granted a dozen Louisiana petrochemical facilities two-year exemptions from a Biden-era rule designed to cut toxic emissions in these same communities (12).

Life expectancy in parts of the Niger Delta, where decades of oil spills have contaminated environment, runs roughly a decade below Nigeria's national average, a pattern echoed in Cancer Alley, where residents already face elevated rates of respiratory illness, reproductive harm, and cancer (13).

European cities are not immune. Warsaw, Poland, has made real progress, cutting fine particulate pollution by 46% since 2010 through coal-heating bans and clean transport zones (14). Yet the city still recorded "unhealthy" air quality spikes in early 2026, and eastern and southeastern Europe as a whole continue to bear the continent's heaviest burden of pollution-linked disease, with nearly all of the EU's urban population still exposed to fine particulate levels above WHO guidelines (15).

Air pollution’s economic impact

Governments rolling back environmental rules often frame the move as an economic win: fewer regulations, lower costs, more jobs. The reality is more complicated.

A tracking project by the Institute for Policy Integrity estimates that just the rollbacks pursued by the current U.S. administration put more than $22 billion in annual health benefits at risk, benefits that would otherwise come from avoided hospital visits, missed workdays, and premature deaths (16).

In Europe, a similar dynamic is unfolding. Corporate lobbying groups representing the automotive, chemical, and fossil fuel industries have spent tens of millions of euros pushing to delay the EU's carbon market reforms and weaken its carbon border tax, arguing that decarbonization rules threaten European competitiveness (17). Yet the same industries benefiting from looser rules are often the ones whose pollution imposes hidden costs on public health systems and the ecosystems their supply chains depend on.

The palm oil industry illustrates the trade-off well. Despite over a decade of "no deforestation" pledges covering most of Indonesia and Malaysia's palm oil refining capacity, satellite monitoring found that more than 31,000 hectares of forest were still cleared for palm oil in Indonesia in 2025 alone, much of it entering supply chains that companies market as deforestation-free (18). Air pollution caused by land clearing for palm plantations impacts air quality in communities across the region each year, despite laws designed to cut emissions (19). The EU's own deforestation regulation, meant to close these loopholes, was delayed a year and then weakened further under industry pressure in late 2025 (20).

Air pollution’s burden falls unevenly

Weakened environmental protections rarely harm everyone equally. Time and again, it is marginalized communities who live closest to the pollution and farthest from the political power to stop it.

In Europe, Roma communities across Hungary, Romania, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and North Macedonia continue to face what researchers call "environmental racism," routinely relocated to or left in areas next to landfills, contaminated industrial sites, and mining waste, often without access to clean water or basic sanitation (21)(22). In one case in Kosovo, the United Nations found that a UN mission itself was responsible for relocating Roma families to a camp near a lead-contaminated industrial site, where residents suffered acute lead poisoning and miscarriages for years without compensation (23).

Indigenous communities face similar patterns on a global scale. In Brazil, more than a third of the Amazon is designated Indigenous territory, and Indigenous-managed lands consistently show lower deforestation rates than surrounding areas (24). Yet Brazil's new self-licensing law and a legal doctrine limiting land claims to territory physically occupied as of 1988 threaten to strip protections from communities that were forcibly displaced decades earlier (25).

In Nigeria's Niger Delta, Ogoni communities are still fighting for a promised cleanup of oil contamination that a 2011 UN assessment estimated could take up to 35 years, even as the Nigerian government pushes to resume drilling in the same region (26). In Canada and Australia, Indigenous groups similarly report being sidelined from decisions about mining, agriculture, and land development on or near traditional territories, often bearing the environmental costs of projects they had little say in approving.

Ecosystems under mounting pressure

The ecological toll of weakened protections is playing out across some of the planet's most iconic landscapes.

In the Arctic, sea ice reached its lowest winter maximum extent in the 47-year satellite record in March 2025, a stark marker of a warming polar region even as summer melt patterns show some natural variability (27)(28). The long-term trend remains unambiguous: sea ice is thinner, younger, and less extensive than it was two decades ago, with cascading effects on global weather patterns and Indigenous communities whose ways of life are tied to the ice (29).

New Zealand is confronting what one 2025 government report called a "code red for nature." More than 4,000 native species are now threatened or at risk of extinction, including 76% of freshwater fish and 93% of frogs, driven largely by intensive dairy farming, habitat loss, and pollution of waterways (30)(31). Conservation groups warn that the government's recent move to weaken indigenous biodiversity and freshwater protections, making it easier to approve mining and quarrying, will accelerate a decline that is already among the worst in the world.

What can be done

The scale of these rollbacks can feel overwhelming, but the trend is not irreversible. Meaningful progress is still possible at every level.

What governments can do

Strengthen and enforce international environmental agreements rather than allowing them to be quietly weakened through delay and exemption.

Invest in environmental monitoring systems that don't rely on industry self-reporting.

Provide financial and technical support to developing nations working to build cleaner energy and industrial systems.

Promote the transfer of green technology so that economic development and environmental protection are not treated as competing goals.

What communities can do

Build cross-border alliances with communities facing similar pollution and land-rights challenges.

Support independent water and air quality monitoring organizations, particularly where government data relies on self-reporting from polluters.

Educate community members about environmental risks and their legal rights to challenge harmful projects.

Develop or support local air quality monitoring networks that can hold industry accountable with independent data.

What individuals can do

Reduce personal carbon footprint where possible, from waste, transportation choices to energy use.

Support businesses and political leaders with genuine track records on environmental responsibility.

Stay informed about local and national policy changes that affect environmental protections.

The takeaway

Weakening environmental protections is a human issue, which carries immediate consequences for human health and long-term consequences for ecosystem. When protections erode, the costs land hardest on communities with the least power to resist them.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) issued an emergency order Sunday to keep Americans across 17 states powered as hot weather conditions continue.

What we know:

The order directs Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) to dispatch generator units to operate as a last resort as needed to maintain electric service in the SPP East and West Balancing Authority Areas (BAAs) in the following 17 states:

Texas

Louisiana

Arkansas

Missouri

Iowa

North Dakota

South Dakota

Nebraska

Oklahoma

Kansas

Colorado

Wyoming

Montana

New Mexico

Arizona

Minnesota

Utah

Dig deeper:

The DOE says the order was issued after a request from SPP and directs SPP to dispatch specified generation units and to order their operation as needed to maintain reliability as a last resort before declaring an Energy Emergency Alert 3 (EEA 3), one of the final steps before rolling outages are implemented.

DOE says they estimate there are more than 35 gigawatts (GW) of unused backup generation remaining available nationwide.

What they're saying:

"The Trump Administration is tapping into an abundant supply of unused backup generation to maintain affordable, reliable, and secure power for hardworking American families and businesses," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright in a release.

Big picture view:

The Southwest Power Poll (SPP) is a Regional Transmission Organization headquartered in Little Rock, Arkansas and mandated by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). SPP ensures there are reliable power supplies and manages the electic transmission infrastructure across a multistate territory.

Earlier this year, SPP expanded its territory into the Western Interconnection, integrating utilities across seven states including parts of Arizona, Colorado, and Utah.

text:
Courier Journal reporters Olivia Evans and Connor Giffin have been honored with a national award in the 2026 SPJ Green Eyeshade Awards.

The reporting duo won first place in the 2026 Business and Technology Reporting category for their investigation into unsafe working conditions at the now-shuttered BlueOval SK electric vehicle battery maker plant, in Glendale, Kentucky.

The Green Eyeshade Awards, celebrating its 76th year, recognize excellent in print, television, radio and digital media across the southeastern U.S. Running since 1950 and hosted by the Society of Professional Journalists, it is the oldest and largest regional contest of its kind.

"This recognition is a tremendous honor for Olivia, Connor and The Courier Journal. I am proud to see this investigation that gave voice to workers and held the company accountable recognized at this level," said Courier Journal Executive Editor and VP for local news, Mary Irby-Jones.

The BlueOval SK investigation focused on workers that raised safety concerns, ranging from chemical exposure to injury and respiratory illness, at the Glendale plant and the numerous state labor investigations centered on the plant based on those worker complaints.

Months later, BlueOval SK announced it was shuttering the Kentucky plant, resulting in job losses for more than 1,500 workers. The company's $5.8 billion site in Hardin County was in production for only four months.

description:
Leading low-carbon liquid fuels (LCLF) company HAMR Energy has welcomed up to $32 million in conditional funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) to advance its landmark projects that will transform Australian plantation forestry residues and renewable energy into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), helping decarbonize one of the country’s most critical and hardest-to-abate sectors.
The projects will strengthen Australia’s fuel security by establishing an integrated domestic supply chain for low-carbon liquid fuels using Australian renewable energy and plantation forestry residues.
Feasibility work has been completed and HAMR Energy is progressing into Front-End Engineering Design and further development activities across the supply chain.
ARENA will provide $12.5 million for the initial phase, with a further $19.5 million to support detailed FEED once HAMR has secured required project co-funding.
HAMR Energy expects to create hundreds of construction jobs and more than 200 ongoing roles, while supporting new opportunities across plantation forestry, renewable energy, engineering, manufacturing and regional supply chains.
text:
Leading low-carbon liquid fuels (LCLF) company HAMR Energy has welcomed up to $32 million in conditional funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) to advance its landmark projects that will transform Australian plantation forestry residues and renewable energy into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), helping decarbonize one of the country’s most critical and hardest-to-abate sectors.

The funding was announced at Adelaide Airport by the Hon Catherine King MP, Minister for Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government and the Hon Chris Bowen MP, Minister for Climate Change and Energy. Also in attendance were the Hon Peter Malinauskas MP, Premier of South Australia and the Hon Chris Picton MP, South Australian Minister for State Development.

The commitment is the first investment under the Australian Government’s $250 million Low Carbon Liquid Fuels priority, administered by ARENA through the Future Made in Australia Innovation Fund, supporting the development of a new domestic industry capable of producing lower-emissions fuels for aviation and other hard-to-abate sectors.

Spanning South Australia and Victoria, the projects are anchored by Australia’s first large-scale methanol-to-jet SAF refinery in Port Adelaide. The funding will support engineering and development work across the integrated supply chain, from aggregating plantation forestry residues in the Green Triangle and producing low-carbon methanol through to the production of SAF, renewable diesel and other fuels.

The projects will strengthen Australia’s fuel security by establishing an integrated domestic supply chain for low-carbon liquid fuels using Australian renewable energy and plantation forestry residues. Anchored by Australia’s first proposed large-scale methanol-to-jet SAF refinery in Port Adelaide, the project would establish sovereign domestic production capability and reduce reliance on imported liquid fuels.

At full scale, HAMR Energy’s projects have the potential to process approximately 600,000 metric tons of plantation forestry residues each year to produce around 300,000 metric tons of low-carbon methanol. The Port Adelaide refinery would convert that methanol into approximately 140 million liters of SAF annually, alongside renewable diesel and other low carbon fuels.

Crucially, this volume of SAF could displace approximately 140 million liters of fossil fuels, abate around 390,000 metric tons of CO2 equivalent per annum and also facilitate approximately 4.5 million economy passenger trips between Adelaide and Melbourne each year.

Feasibility work has been completed and HAMR Energy is progressing into Front-End Engineering Design and further development activities across the supply chain. ARENA will provide $12.5 million for the initial phase, with a further $19.5 million to support detailed FEED once HAMR has secured required project co-funding.

HAMR Energy expects to create hundreds of construction jobs and more than 200 ongoing roles, while supporting new opportunities across plantation forestry, renewable energy, engineering, manufacturing and regional supply chains.

text:
The Clean Energy Generation is making progress every day here in the Southeast. From Tallahassee opening EV charging stations, to Atlanta giving out e-bike rebates, to Loretto switching to LED streetlights, our clean energy future is becoming a reality. Take a look at just six of the many local signs of clean energy adoption we’ve seen in the Southeast so far this year.

Chatham County Slashes Utility Bills by Cutting Energy Waste

Ratepayers in Chatham County, Georgia have seen a 30% increase in their electric bills in just three years. Now, in an effort to cut energy waste and slash utility bills, the county is targeting high-energy-use municipal buildings for energy efficient upgrades — from new light bulbs to more intensive retrofits. Identified targets include the county’s civil rights museum, aquatic center, and former courthouse. Read more.

Tallahassee Opens Its First Flagship EV Charging Station

Tallahassee is plugging into the future. The city recently opened its first flagship EV charging station near Florida A&M University. Two additional charging stations are already in the works, one across the road from the Southside Transit Center and another on West Tharpe Street near North MLK Boulevard. All three chargers are part of the city’s goal to use 100% clean energy by 2050. Read more.

Atlanta E-bike Rebate Program Curbs Driving by 40%

Atlanta’s e-bike rebate program returned for another year after a successful launch. Previous rebate recipients, who each received between $500 and $2,000 for a standard or cargo e-bike, drove a whopping 40% less each week. In addition to keeping cars off the road, the program also boosted locally owned bike shops. The 12 participating shops saw a $1.2 million jump in sales. Read more.

Loretto Switches All of Its Streetlights to LED

Talk about a bright idea! The city of Loretto, Tennessee is switching all of its streetlights to LED fixtures. The energy-efficient switch will not only illuminate larger areas and improve public safety, but will also reduce maintenance costs and save taxpayers money. The project will even replace the lights at the city’s baseball and softball fields. Read more.

Alpharetta Police Department Opens Four EV Fast Chargers

One Georgia police department is charging ahead. The city of Alpharetta recently opened four EV fast chargers at the city’s police headquarters. Delivering about 200 miles of range in just 15 minutes, these chargers will not only power the department’s electric patrol vehicles, but will also increase charging accessibility for the entire community. Read more.

Raleigh Sees an Increase in Public Transit Ridership

Trading pumps for passes. As gas prices rise, the public transit system serving North Carolina’s Raleigh-Durham-Chapel Hill area has seen an increase in ridership. April brought a 32% bump in riders compared to 2025, while March brought a 28% bump. Several people can ride the bus for free, including adults who receive Medicaid, SNAP or EBT benefits, or have a household income below $35,000. Read more.

Follow along each week

These stories highlight just a few of the positive things happening in our area! Every day, we see signs of hope. The Clean Energy Generation is creating a future powered by clean energy that leads to clean air and water, good jobs, and vibrant communities.

Would you like to see more stories like this? We’ve got just the thing for you! Every Thursday, we share the latest clean energy news on Instagram with #CleanEnergyNews. Join us as we celebrate the progress and signs of hope in the clean energy transition.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Google, Ford, Carhartt and BlackRock launched a partnership last week designed to expand access to training programs for skilled trades.

The initiative, which the companies call the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, will look to broaden access to vocational careers and build awareness of the types of jobs that will be needed to support critical industries like infrastructure, energy and manufacturing, according to a July 21 press release.

Recent research from commercial real estate company JLL shows that a shortfall of trade workers could translate to more than 2.1 million unfilled positions for electricians, HVAC technicians, plumbers, pipefitters, construction equipment operators and general maintenance workers by 2030.

Dive Insight:

BlackRock found that the employment in infrastructure-related jobs — including welders, carpenters, HVAC, electricians, plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters — is expected to grow 5% from 2024-34, faster than the 3% projected national average employment growth, based on outlooks for the fields from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A separate report from McKinsey & Company found that skilled labor shortages, geopolitical shifts and other factors are increasing investment needs and “changing how infrastructure is planned, financed, and executed.” The report also estimates that up to $85 trillion will be needed in investments to support infrastructure for the transportation, energy, digital, water and waste sectors over the next 15 years.

The four founding alliance members have independently committed to support workforce training initiatives across 30 states, according to the press release. Together, the group said its goals are to build a “skilled trades pipeline” and scale up workforce development approaches including apprenticeships and pre-apprenticeship programs.

“Building the physical infrastructure for America’s future requires significantly increasing the pipeline of skilled tradespeople across the country — a challenge that can only be addressed with collective action,” Google President and Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat said in the release.

In its efforts to expand the pipeline of skilled trades workers, the alliance said it will look to provide “clear, accessible pathways” and partner with education and workforce training organizations Jobs for the Future and the Burning Glass Institute on a report to identify where gaps exist, measure progress and share best practices. The alliance said it will also look to expand to “like-minded industry, labor, education, and nonprofit organizations.”

There were 600,000 jobs posted for skilled trades in 2025, but only 150,000 people entered the labor pool through apprenticeships, according to JLL’s report. The company added that still-rising college tuitions, $1.8 trillion in student loan debt and disruption from artificial intelligence are “reshaping career decisions.”

Research from the Department of Education found that labor shortages and skills gaps are “especially acute in manufacturing, construction, and other skilled trades,” sectors where for every five workers who retire, only two replacements enter the workforce.

The DOE has estimated that the shortfall of skilled trade workers could lead to up to $1 trillion in annual economic losses.

Ford President and CEO Jim Farley said in the release that the automaker sees the skilled workforce shortage as “a national crisis but also a generational opportunity.”

text:
President Donald Trump’s decision to impose 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods is escalating a trade confrontation at precisely the wrong moment for U.S. energy security.

The measures target products including alcohol, dairy, furniture, cement, paper and… hockey sticks. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the duties the latest in "a series of tariffs in direct violation" of the CUSMA trade agreement.

For now, Canada’s most consequential export to the U.S.—crude oil—remains exempt. That matters enormously. Canadian shipments account for about 62% of U.S. oil imports and more than a quarter of crude processed by domestic refineries. Alberta alone sends about 85% of its exports south, largely energy.

But an exemption is increasingly looking like a temporary political carve-out rather than a durable settlement. Trump’s decision to apply levies to products covered by USMCA signals an intention to broaden the trade arsenal. Prediction market odds of a new U.S.-Canada trade agreement in 2026 have fallen to only 9%.

Shaky Global Energy Market

That situation raises the prospect of a collision between Trump’s trade agenda and his pledge to keep fuel affordable.

Global markets offer no easy substitute. Tankers face threats through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb passage and the Black Sea. Brent briefly topped $100 a barrel last week as attacks and blockades disrupted shipping.

Meanwhile, strategic petroleum reserve releases that helped dampen prices are running down, and global inventories are tightening.

"The U.S. has essentially run out of spare refining capacity—it’s refining just about as much as it possibly can," Gregory Brew, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said according to Politico. That leaves refiners with little ability to offset a new supply shock.

Midwest Refiners Face Risks

The first corporate casualties of a loss of Canada’s oil exemption would be U.S. refiners built around heavy Canadian crude.

Marathon Petroleum Corp. (NYSE:MPC) , Phillips 66 (NYSE:PSX) and Valero Energy Corp. (NYSE:VLO) have invested heavily in complex plants designed to process discounted heavy barrels from Alberta.

Marathon’s Detroit and Robinson facilities, as well as Phillips 66’s Wood River refinery, depend on steady pipeline flows from Canada. Replacing those barrels wouldn’t be seamless. Domestic supplies are generally lighter, while imported heavy crude would have to compete for increasingly disrupted seaborne routes.

That shift would squeeze refinery margins or raise wholesale fuel costs—or both. In a market with little spare processing capacity, the burden would quickly move from corporate balance sheets to service-station signs.

U.S. gasoline prices climbed 15 cents in a week to $4.09 a gallon, according to AAA, as the broader oil crisis intensified. Brew has warned prices could reach $5 a gallon if disruptions persist into the fall.

Trump’s tariff escalation seems aimed at extracting better terms from Ottawa. Yet putting Canadian crude in the crosshairs would risk turning an already fragile global energy emergency into a made-in-Washington price shock, one American drivers and Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms would be hard-pressed to ignore.

title: Building performance standards have deadlines and penalties — are you ready for them?
authors: Robert Freedman, Joe Burns, Julia Himmel, Christy Martell
description:
Christy Martell is senior vice president at IES, a building performance software company.
For the past several years, building performance standards have mainly been a topic for architects, energy modelers and policy advocates.
That’s a problem, because in some jurisdictions, the compliance deadlines are arriving, along with the penalties for not meeting them.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Christy Martell is senior vice president at IES, a building performance software company. Opinions are the author’s own.

For the past several years, building performance standards have mainly been a topic for architects, energy modelers and policy advocates. The conversations have happened at design charrettes, in code update meetings and at sustainability conferences. The assumption running through most of those conversations is that if the design community gets it right, the compliance problem takes care of itself.

That assumption is wrong, and many building owners are starting to find that out.

Building performance standards — the new generation of regulations that go beyond prescriptive energy codes to hold buildings accountable for their operational performance — are landing on the desks of facility managers, many of whom were not involved in the original design decisions.

That’s a problem, because in some jurisdictions, the compliance deadlines are arriving, along with the penalties for not meeting them. In many cases, the people now responsible for hitting those targets haven’t been the ones looking into what the targets are.

Addressing that knowledge gap starts with visibility: learning what the building’s performance is, how far it sits from the target and which systems are driving the gap. But it’s not enough just to know these things; you need to know them early enough so you can get the building to the targets.

Compliance landscape

Although a number of jurisdictions have pushed back some or all of their deadlines, compliance requirements are still moving forward. In Boston, for example, the city has pushed back its original reporting deadline from May 15 to August 15. And Denver has pushed back its interim and final target deadlines to 2028 and 2032, respectively. Facility managers will want to familiarize themselves with what their jurisdiction is doing if they’re facing compliance deadlines.

New York City’s Local Law 97, the most aggressive building performance mandate in the country, applies to buildings larger than 25,000 square feet and sets carbon intensity limits that tighten significantly in 2030. The first compliance period began in 2024 and fines are $268 per metric ton of CO2e above the building’s limit.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Facilities Dive free daily newsletter

It’s not just New York where strict standards are being enforced: Washington, D.C.’s Building Energy Performance Standards require applicable buildings to meet the city’s first compliance cycle by the end of 2026; Boston’s Building Emissions Reduction and Disclosure Ordinance (BERDO) will soon be ramping down its emissions limits; and Denver’s Energize Denver program has imposed performance targets on its largest buildings, subject to the timeline changes.

Chicago, Philadelphia, and a growing list of other cities are also either implementing or developing their own standards. The pattern is consistent: mandates applied first to the largest properties, then stepping down to smaller buildings in subsequent years.

The design-operations gap

Most building performance standards were written with the design community as the primary audience. The framing assumes that compliance is achieved through good design, efficient systems and smart specifications, and that’s partly true. The decisions made at the design stage create either headroom or constraint for the operational team that follows.

But design teams move on. The architect and MEP engineer who optimized the HVAC system for energy performance way back when are not the ones answering for an LL97 fine in 2026. That responsibility belongs to whoever manages the building today, often working with systems they didn’t select, operating under assumptions they weren’t part of making and sometimes running buildings that were never properly commissioned in the first place.

Read More in Sustainability

What operations teams need to track

The starting point is energy use intensity. That is the building’s annual energy consumption per square foot, expressed in kBtu/sf, or in carbon terms, depending on the jurisdiction. Most facility managers have access to this data through utility bills and ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, which is the benchmarking platform that most jurisdictions use as their BPS compliance framework.

Portfolio Manager gives the facilities team a headline energy use intensity, or EUI, that tells you how much energy the building is using per square foot. That’s useful as a compliance yardstick, but what it doesn’t do is tell you which systems are responsible, whether the pattern is changing and where the corrective lever actually is.

The operations teams making real headway are the ones going a level deeper. Rather than waiting for an annual utility bill summary, they’re pulling consumption data continuously, comparing it against what the building’s systems should be consuming based on how the building is being used — occupancy levels, weather, operating schedules — rather than against a historical average that may reflect a period when the building was running just as inefficiently.

That kind of performance monitoring, tied to the physics of the building rather than just the meter, is what separates a team that can identify and close a gap from one that is watching a compliance number it can’t explain. Platforms built specifically for building performance connect operational data to engineering-grade building models, so when a performance problem surfaces, there’s enough context to act on it rather than just observe it.

Read More in Sustainability

Beyond the headline figure, the data that enables corrective action is more granular. Which systems are driving consumption? How does performance vary across seasons and occupancy levels? Are there equipment inefficiencies, control failures or operational patterns pushing energy use higher than it should be?

Understanding the shape of a building’s energy consumption — not just the total — is what separates a team that can improve its position from one that is simply watching a number it can’t explain.

For multi-site portfolios, the challenge compounds. Different buildings face different deadlines, different local ordinances and different benchmarks depending on use type. A mixed portfolio spanning multiple jurisdictions needs a clear map of what’s required where and by when, not a generalized sense that compliance is being handled.

The window for early intervention is closing

Buildings facing the nearest deadlines are already in the compliance window. For them, the margin for operational correction — adjusting schedules, optimizing controls, addressing deferred maintenance, improving occupancy management — is real, and shrinking. Capital improvements take time to plan, fund and execute.

For buildings with deadlines a few years further out, the opportunity is better. Getting a clear baseline now, understanding the gap between performance and the applicable target and building a realistic improvement pathway gives operations teams something to work with rather than a deadline to scramble toward.

name: Indiana Environment
title: Can energy efficiency help solve affordability woes in Indiana? - Daily Journal
description:
For now, the clearest path to more energy efficient local governments is to consider efficiency in new projects, he said.
“It’s largely because of energy efficiency, building codes, appliance standards that for all intents and purposes we’ve seen flat energy demand up until the last few years,” he said.
Jaworowski said energy efficiency is a big priority for the Braun administration, but so is pushing more energy supply onto the grid.
Energy efficiency “is something that you can do immediately.” Even without significant “sticks,” most utilities are pursuing energy efficiency as part of meeting growing demands.
The utility’s 11 different energy efficiency programs play an important role in managing even the lower demand scenarios in its most recent Integrated Resource Plan, said Hammond.
text:
The issue is multifaceted, but in Indiana, it has presented itself most recently in rising electricity rates.

Last month, Gov. Mike Braun replaced the chair of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission after the agency approved a base rate increase for AES and asked the state’s Office of Utility Consumer Counselor to file for a rehearing — which it later did.

Regulators are now set to further consider claims between consumer advocates and AES over who should pay for a list of costs.

Even if the IURC reverses its decision, electricity prices from AES — and across the state — will remain higher than they were just a few years ago. Prices have consistently risen over the past two decades, but there has been a large bump since 2020.

One solution that could help counter the higher costs: finding ways to use less electricity by making buildings more efficient.

“The cheapest electrons are the ones we never have to generate in the first place,” said Adam Hammond, AES Indiana’s customer program manager.

That’s a widely held view among government officials, businesses and advocacy groups.

But the path to less usage is not always intuitive.

The “Indiana Energy Playbook,” released in June, by Indiana University’s Paul H. O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs, argues that energy efficiency upgrades can be an important tool for local governments to cut costs as the state limits their taxing authority — another aspect of the affordability crunch.

The Indiana University report also provides a roadmap for local governments to make city-owned infrastructure more efficient and actions that can be taken to help local residents and businesses do the same.

Still, getting to that more efficient — and ultimately cheaper — system can be expensive in the interim.

Taking stock

Government promotion of energy efficiency is nothing new. There have been programs encouraging these types of measures for decades, and Indiana electric utilities are required to submit plans that outline their own to the IURC at least every three years.

But countless buildings across the state could stand to make relatively small tweaks — like improving insulation or installing “smart thermostats” that set temperatures for different times of the day — that could result in big savings.

This is especially true for government buildings in small towns, said Riley Welsh, a McKinney Climate Fellow with Indiana Conservation Voters who helped write the report as an Indiana University graduate student.

“We were seeing smaller towns with older buildings can get 60-70% energy savings with weatherization and smart thermostats,” Welsh said.

Each time a building is made more efficient it saves the ratepayer money, but it also reduces strain on the broader power grid.

“When you’re talking about thousands of those smart thermostats across our system, in that aggregate, they have a large impact,” Hammond said.

And that ultimately drives down prices for everyone, since it can help prevent utilities like AES from going to the market to purchase additional and expensive energy during times of peak demand, Hammond said.

With municipalities, energy savings can add up fast due to the large number of buildings they operate, Welsh said.

But it can be hard to know where to get started, said Welsh. The Energy Playbook recommends that cities conduct audits of their buildings, allowing them to take stock of where things stand.

That’s what is underway in Indianapolis right now.

A federal grant of $787,000 awarded in late 2024 is allowing the city to audit the efficiency of its infrastructure.

Some of that money will eventually be used to implement some suggestions from the audits, said Indianapolis Sustainability Office Community Engagement Manager Mads Gullion.

With more than 200 city-owned buildings to go through, the audits are a big task within themselves.

“The biggest challenge we’ve encountered so far is just how disparate [the buildings] are and how they’re run by different departments and maintained by different people,” Gullion said.

State government has its own federally funded efficiency effort — the $182 million Energy Savers Program, run through the Office of Energy Development — aimed at helping lower- and middle-income households make efficiency upgrades.

Since its rollout in May 2025, more than 1,000 households across all 92 counties in the state have signed up, said Indiana Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources Suzanne Jaworowski.

“We have contractors out right now working with homeowners and helping them evaluate things like: Do you have enough insulation in your attic? Are your windows sealed up tight? How are your appliances?” she said.

The average participating household has reduced their energy consumption by more than 25%, Jaworowski said.

“It was popular from the word, ‘go,’” she said.

‘All carrot’

While in the long-term, energy efficiency improvements generally pay off, making those investments can be a challenge for cash-strapped local governments, said Accelerate Indiana Municipalities CEO Matt Greller.

“When you’re looking at significant cuts to property taxes and income taxes, the two primary ways you fund local government, it’s hard to get much beyond just doing the basics,” he said.

For now, the clearest path to more energy efficient local governments is to consider efficiency in new projects, he said.

“It does take years to see the full benefit of going with the more efficient, and it does come in relatively small increments,” Greller said. “But every little bit [of savings] is going to help.”

The challenge of paying off upfront capital costs for upgrades is evident with another program partly administered by the city of Indianapolis.

The Thriving Nonprofits program provides matching grants of up to $10,000 from the McKinney Family Foundation for nonprofits seeking more efficient facilities. A total of $300,000 was spent on audits and an array of different efficiency upgrades across 10 projects in the first cohort, said Gullion.

That has resulted in energy savings of about $36,500 in the first year, said Gullion. That’s significant savings, but it will still take years to make up for the initial investment.

However, as energy prices are projected to increase, those efficiency upgrades will likely pay for themselves quicker, Gullion noted.

Lowering systemwide demands also reduces the need for utility companies to build more infrastructure, which is ultimately paid for by customers, said Kerwin Olson, executive director at Citizens Action Coalition.

“It’s largely because of energy efficiency, building codes, appliance standards that for all intents and purposes we’ve seen flat energy demand up until the last few years,” he said. But he added that “data centers sort of are changing that conversation” because their energy needs dwarf those of all other users.

“One would think with this understanding of load growth coming from data centers that we would double down even more on efficiency,” Olson said.

While the existing efficiency programs of Indiana utilities are “fairly robust,” they could go further, Olson argued.

One reason they don’t is that the state’s efficiency targets — established by former Gov. Mitch Daniels in 2009 — were repealed in 2014. The change allows utilities to set their own standards, Olson said. “I think the issue we have in the state of Indiana right now is it’s all carrot and no stick,” he said.

The state has also stepped in to limit some other efficiency efforts. Earlier this year, the Indiana General Assembly stripped municipalities of their ability to mandate that buildings report utility data. That affected a program in Indianapolis that had the power to impose $100 fines for buildings above 50,000 square feet that did not comply. Despite the change, about 400 buildings participate voluntarily, Gullion said.

Jaworowski said energy efficiency is a big priority for the Braun administration, but so is pushing more energy supply onto the grid.

“Growth is the way to ultimately lower the cost of electricity around the entire state, but that takes time,” she said. Energy efficiency “is something that you can do immediately.”

Even without significant “sticks,” most utilities are pursuing energy efficiency as part of meeting growing demands.

That includes AES. The utility’s 11 different energy efficiency programs play an important role in managing even the lower demand scenarios in its most recent Integrated Resource Plan, said Hammond.

One challenge, he said, is getting information about the programs to customers.

“In every scenario that we modeled in our IRP, energy efficiency was a critical component of making sure that we’re able to deliver safe, adequate and affordable energy at the lowest cost possible,” he said.

name: Clean Energy
title: Energy reliability is what we need to talk about when it comes to power | The Seattle Times
description:
Like most power outages, this one was caused by damage to distribution systems, not power supply shortfalls.
As climate change intensifies wildfires, mortality from acute pulmonary impacts increases, while everyone who breathes suffers worsening health effects.
So why do these real catastrophes seem to get less attention from energy providers than hypothetical and manageable power shortfalls?
Because climate disruption is too damned big — scary, depressing and seemingly beyond our power to make a difference.
We cannot afford “solutions” to manageable energy challenges that make climate disruption unmanageable.
text:
As power-hungry data centers seek to expand and we electrify our vehicles and buildings, warnings about looming electricity shortfalls are growing louder. The concern is real, but much of the recent commentary overemphasizes manageable, moderate risks while ignoring more urgent and costly ones. Weakening clean energy laws to allow more gas power plants, as some have proposed, would throw us from the frying pan into the fire.

Many of these warnings cite the January 2024 cold snap, which strained the electrical grid’s capacity, as a cautionary example. We didn’t fall short of power during that event, but we narrowly avoided “rolling blackouts” — power interruptions that typically last 60-90 minutes to keep supply and demand in balance. Power providers build the electric grid with extra “reserve” capacity so these emergency measures are rarely needed.

But while that specter — a near miss of scheduled power interruptions — is being used to lobby for more gas, much more serious power outages have actually occurred. Last December, nearly 1 million Washingtonians lost power for up to four days due to wind and flooding from an extreme storm that had “the fingerprints of climate change” all over it. Like most power outages, this one was caused by damage to distribution systems, not power supply shortfalls. Building power plants powered by fossil fuels makes these storms and the associated power failures worse, by stoking the climate heating that exacerbates extreme weather.

Another recent catastrophe — the heat dome of 2021 — was amplified and made vastly more likely by climate disruption. It directly or indirectly caused over 400 deaths in Washington. Europe recorded 10,000 excess deaths in this June’s heat wave. As climate change intensifies wildfires, mortality from acute pulmonary impacts increases, while everyone who breathes suffers worsening health effects. As I write, over 100 million Americans are breathing smoke-filled air. Energy choices that prolong fossil fuel dependence make these events more dangerous and costly.

So why do these real catastrophes seem to get less attention from energy providers than hypothetical and manageable power shortfalls?

In the excellent book “Fire Weather,” John Vaillant describes the “Lucretius Effect”: We misperceive risks that are outside our normal frame of reference. I might also suggest a “Serenity Prayer Effect”: In the face of terrible climate news, we seek “serenity to accept the things we cannot change,” forgetting that the prayer also calls for courage to change the things we can and wisdom to know the difference.

Why do we jump to serenity and bypass courage and wisdom?

Because climate disruption is too damned big — scary, depressing and seemingly beyond our power to make a difference. Politics plays a big role too: We see climate change through the distorting lens of political gamesmanship and oil industry deception, rather than the clear, harsh light of objective reality. Many political consultants advise candidates to avoid the topic altogether.

But physics doesn’t play politics. The consequences of fossil fuel dependence are upon us. To respond effectively, we need an accurate sense of proportion about the risks associated with our energy decisions. We cannot afford “solutions” to manageable energy challenges that make climate disruption unmanageable.

This is not to advocate complacency in the face of a prospective energy crunch. It’s a pressing challenge and we need to tackle it. The Northwest Power and Conservation Council, on which I serve as a representative of Washington, is charged with delivering a regional power plan that minimizes costs, balances risks, and maintains a high standard of power resource adequacy.

name: Congress
title: Scientists run for Congress in a stand against climate denialism and threats to Nature
description:
A movement is underway to confront the climate denialism that has dominated the National Congress.
Nevertheless, in addition to Luciana Gatti, here are some of the people running for seats in the Chamber of Deputies: .
“The Bolsonaro administration’s attack on Brazilian science was institutional,” Mariana recalls.
Galvão also points to the cuts Dilma made to the research budget as the start of a mobilization by scientists to run for Congress.
Scientists in Congress are nothing new.
text:
A movement is underway to confront the climate denialism that has dominated the National Congress. Still low-key and somewhat disorganized, it is coming out of research institutions and universities and aims to elect scientists who can, within the Chamber of Deputies, bring reason to decisive debates on the future of life on Earth.

It is evident in pre-candidacies across Brazil, such as that of climate scientist Luciana Vanni Gatti. In an exclusive interview with SUMAÚMA, she summed up why academics are entering the political fray: “We have to do something unplanned, unusual. What Congress is doing [by cutting protections for Nature] will be decisive in accelerating the end of our lives.”

The list of candidates below is incomplete. It was compiled by SUMAÚMA based on conversations with organizations and scientists. A more comprehensive list will emerge once party conventions have ended and candidacies are registered by the Supreme Electoral Court on August 16. Nevertheless, in addition to Luciana Gatti, here are some of the people running for seats in the Chamber of Deputies:

. Ricardo Galvão, the former director of the National Institute for Space Research, previously elected as an alternate federal deputy in 2022 through the Socialism and Liberty Party-Rede federation, who will run again in São Paulo as a candidate for the Brazilian Socialist Party;

. Nísia Trindade, a researcher and the former president of the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation who was formerly a health minister and is now a Workers Party candidate to represent Rio de Janeiro;

. Wilson Cabral de Sousa Júnior, an oceanographer and associate professor of environmental engineering at the Aeronautics Institute of Technology, running with the Democratic Labor Party to represent São Paulo;

. Tatiana Roque, a mathematician and professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, who currently serves as a municipal councilor in Rio de Janeiro and is a candidate for the Brazilian Socialist Party;

. Márcia Abrahão, a geologist and associate professor at the Institute of Geosciences at the University of Brasilia who was the first woman to serve as the dean of the institution (from 2016 to 2024). She is running with the Workers Party to represent the Federal District.

Other men and women, in addition to these candidates, also want to raise the voice of science in state Legislative Assemblies – arenas that have proven at least as prone to far-right denialism as the National Congress.

To understand where this reaction from academia is coming from, we need to go ten years back.

.

“We encourage scientists from every state in the federation to run for a seat in parliament so that, along with the few intellectuals already there, we can build a Knowledge Caucus. […] We need scientists in parliament! Join the Engaged Scientists!” reads a manifesto released in March 2018 by a group of professors and graduate students at universities in São Paulo. There have always been scientist candidates, or parliamentarians who advocated for scientists’ demands, but the idea behind the manifesto was to form a “science caucus,” capable of joining people in Congress who work with science on a daily basis and are willing to fight for science in the Legislature.

The Movement of Engaged Scientists emerged from the debates held during the elections for administrative posts at the University of São Paulo one year prior, in 2017. Its candidates, scientists Ildo Sauer and Tércio Ambrizzi, lost.

The main agenda at the time was to counter the cuts to funding for scientific research put in place by Dilma Rousseff (Workers Party) during her second term and made worse by her successor, Michel Temer (Brazilian Democratic Movement). Yet this quickly changed with the election of the far-right Jair Bolsonaro, elected at the time under the Social Liberal Party (which later merged with the Democratas party to create the União Brasil party), and who is currently with the Liberal Party.

“In 2018, we had a debate [on how] ‘the government isn’t paying as much attention to science as it should.’ In 2019, it was ‘we need to defend the institution of science from government attacks,’” explains Mariana Moura, a substitute professor with the Economics Department at São Paulo State University’s Araraquara campus and the founder of Engaged Scientists. “We went from one situation of trying to find advancements to another of staving off regression.”

That year, Mariana took her chances as a candidate for the São Paulo state Legislative Assembly with the miniscule Pátria Livre Party – she paired up with biologist, archeologist, and evolutionary anthropologist Walter Neves, who ran for federal deputy and is one of the people responsible for studies on the oldest skeleton found in the Americas, known as Luzia. Neither was elected. Luzia burned and was partially destroyed in a fire that laid waste to the National Museum in Rio de Janeiro in September 2018 – “It already caught on fire, what do you want me to do?” Bolsonaro said with a shrug when asked to comment on the tragedy.

“The Bolsonaro administration’s attack on Brazilian science was institutional,” Mariana recalls. “His group persecuted deans and faculty to the point of [some] having to leave the country for fear of their own and their families’ lives. And this grew much worse during the pandemic. In 2020, I think every scientist in Brazil began to notice the pressing need for the academic sector to become more involved in the country’s political debates.”

A reaction began to take shape in 2022. The Brazilian Academy of Sciences published a manifesto on its website signed by “former deans, researchers, professors, and leaders who introduced themselves to society as pre-candidates for the national Congress and state Legislative Assemblies.” The dozens of signatories to the document advocated for “Education and Science as fundamental pillars to rebuild Brazil,” in opposition to the “obscurantism [of] a government that denies science in each of its actions.” One of them was Ricardo Galvão, who was driven out of the National Institute for Space Research after defending the accuracy of data on deforestation in the Amazon that had been questioned by Jair Bolsonaro.

Galvão also points to the cuts Dilma made to the research budget as the start of a mobilization by scientists to run for Congress. “But it really grew stronger during the period of denialism [by Bolsonaro regarding the Covid-19 pandemic],” he explains. Elected as an alternate federal deputy, his term began in October 2025 after Guilherme Boulos (Socialism and Liberty Party) vacated his seat. During his time in the Chamber, he attended debates like the one that overrode the line-item vetoes to the Devastation Bill to create a law that hollowed out environmental licensing in Brazil.

“There is quite a strong feeling in society that the quality of Congress is declining significantly,” Galvão says. “With the infamous Devastation Bill, [we saw] people [in Congress] who said global heating doesn’t exist. Denialism is widely used to insert [fabricated] controversies into those scientific debates that hinder the interests of political groups, lobby groups. I saw this clearly in Congress.” Galvão’s critiques of a markedly right-wing parliament cannot be explained by party bias: the scientist was affiliated with the Brazilian Social Democratic Party (he never exercised political activity for the party) from 1993 to 2022 – a time when it was the main adversary of the Workers Party. He moved from there to Marina Silva’s Rede party, and in March of this year he switched to the Brazilian Socialist Party, whose most prominent member is vice president Geraldo Alckmin, who also used to be affiliated with the Brazilian Social Democratic Party.

“It is absolutely necessary to fight for substantial improvement of our Congress, so we can aspire to a dignified and prosperous future for our nation. […] What there is, on the one hand, is a government that gets it right and wrong, it deserves to be watched and held accountable, but it remains within democratic rules. […] On the other hand, however, it’s not just a conservative or liberal alternative. It includes a dangerous mix of resentment, intolerance, disdain for marginalized people, a perverse use of disinformation, and denialist activism. For these reasons, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve decided to enter the political fight again with the goal of bringing scientific rationale to the Federal Chamber,” Ricardo Galvão said in a speech on July 8, National Science Day.

“Denialism is a [political] project. In the case of Brazil, it was a government policy during the pandemic. Scientists in Congress are nothing new. But today, what sets us apart [in the election contest] is the fight against denialism,” says Nísia Trindade, a former president of the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation who served as health minister from 2023 to March 2025 – and is now a federal deputy pre-candidate.

During the Bolsonaro administration, Nísia was on the frontline of the negotiation that allowed the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation to manufacture the Covid-19 vaccine developed by Oxford University and sold by laboratory AstraZeneca. “Congress played a very positive role at that time,” she recalls. In the Health Ministry, however, things became more difficult, the result of a combination of explicit denialism and a parliament puffed up by pork barrel politics. “It has created a very tough situation,” she says. Added to this is the fact that “many parliamentarians go [to debates] ‘to score [political] points’ and [then they] leave.” The belief that these two factors are bulking up Congressional power, while at the same time draining the money that should go to public policies on health, education, and scientific development is shared by every other scientist who spoke with SUMAÚMA for this story – and it is driving candidates to the Chamber of Deputy.

.

A cable-stayed bridge, an object of desire and ostentation for city halls in every corner of Brazil, is what propelled oceanographer and Aeronautics Institute of Technology professor Wilson Cabral de Sousa Júnior into political life. He was a member of the Municipal Environment Council in São José dos Campos, a municipality in the Paraíba Valley of São Paulo, when he came across a project for one of these bridges. Wilson drafted a technical assessment showing the bridge, proposed by the mayor at the time, Felicio Ramuth (Brazilian Democratic Movement), would not solve traffic problems, it would be overly expensive, and – most seriously – work was starting without an environmental license.

“This made the mayor a bit upset,” Wilson recalls. Ramuth is currently the vice governor of São Paulo, serving under the state’s Bolsonarist governor, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos party). There was blowback. “The dean of the Aeronautics Institute of Technology called me [and said] the mayor wanted me out,” he says. It was January 2019, early in the Bolsonaro administration. Wilson, whose actions were defended by the institute’s dean, says he “would have been acting in bad faith [if I had not warned about the project’s problems,] because I’m a public employee.”

The dispute led the professor and two other colleagues to give up their seats on the Council, as they called out the way that “educational and research institutes have been used merely to legitimize” the actions taken by city hall. Rather than driving him away from the public debate, the episode had the opposite effect. In 2024, Wilson ran for mayor under the Democratic Labor Party. He garnered 8,710 votes (2.38% of the total) in a polarized election between a Bolsonarist and Ramuth’s former deputy mayor – who ended up winning the election in the second round of voting. In 2026, Wilson will try for a seat in the Chamber of Deputies.

His time with the Environment Council in São José dos Campos, followed by the passage of the Devastation Bill, gave Wilson the growing impression that the weakening of environmental licensing will create a string of problems – ones he expects to be able to tackle as a federal deputy. “The municipalities don’t have the capacity to do this, but here in the Paraíba Valley, they’re already requesting licenses for high-impact projects – and with very little transparency,” he explains. “If we’re talking about climate change, one of the bottlenecks we have is adaptation [of cities]. The municipalities have very little capacity, even [little] knowledge to deal with this issue,” he says.

(The case of the cable-stayed bridge reached the Federal Supreme Court, which upheld a ruling forcing the municipal government to make several adaptations to the structure based on studies showing the project’s capacity to resolve traffic problems would be exceeded in 2025. The bridge cost approximately 10.6 million dollars.)

.

Founded in 1948, the Brazilian Society for the Progress of Science, “represents 161 affiliate scientific societies and thousands of active members, including researchers, faculty, students, and Brazilian citizens interested in science and technology,” according to its official website. It is for precisely this reason that the society has historically resisted taking a clear political position that was not in defense of science – and, since the business-military dictatorship that ran from 1964 to 1985, of democracy.

According to the current president of the Brazilian Society for the Progress of Science, Francilene Procópio Garcia, “we represent a quite plural scientific community, which should cross the entire political spectrum.” She holds a PhD in electrical engineering and is a professor and researcher at the Federal University of Campina Grande, in Paraíba.

In 2017, in a country plunged into the political crisis resulting from Operation Car Wash and with resources for science dramatically reduced, the society at one point discussed whether it was time for scientists to run for elected office. “This led to an understanding that [it was not time for them to run, but rather] it was better to join those who had already been elected,” Mariana Moura, the coordinator of Engaged Scientists, recalls.

Then came the Bolsonaro years, the Covid-19 pandemic, and worsening of the climate emergency. “The denialism in the health crisis, the drop in vaccine coverage, the dismantling of the main fund supporting science, which is the National Fund for Scientific and Technological Development, the attack on public universities, [all of this] led the Brazilian Society for the Progress of Science to consider the importance that candidates like these, who spent most of their careers in science, could have,” Francilene argues.

“It is legitimate and desirable for us to have researchers who can occupy a relevant space to advocate for science,” the society’s president says. “We have complex transformations on the planet, the differential climate regime, situations where we need a lot of science so we can manage to face these things and overcome them.” The change had already materialized in 2022, with the launch of a compilation of proposals entitled the “Project for a New Brazil.” It served as the inspiration for a new volume, named “The Brazil We Want: Science, Democracy, and Sovereignty,” which brings together proposals from scientists – including Nísia Trindade – collected from a series of roundtables and discussions.

“Without democracy, there is no free science. Without science, there is no sustainable democracy,” according to the letter introducing the document, which sums up the angst of scientists in relation to the explicit denialism from the nation’s Congress. Mariana Moura has a more direct appeal: “Elect scientists. We need science inside Congress.”

text:
$1 million in grants will support nearly 50 North Carolina organizations expanding food access, housing stability, senior services and utility assistance for families, seniors and vulnerable residents

More than $34.6 million to support community needs and $31 million in utility-bill assistance through Share the Light Fund® and Share the Warmth since 2016

Charlotte, N.C. – The Duke Energy Foundation is investing $1 million in nonprofit organizations across North Carolina that help families, seniors and vulnerable residents access essentials such as food, housing, health care, utility assistance and other critical services. The grants will support front line organizations working to support community needs while helping them build the capacity to serve even more people.

Where the money goes: The $1 million investment supports two complementary efforts: helping nonprofits build long-term capacity while expanding services for North Carolina's growing senior population.

Capacity Building: $500,000 will help strengthen 27 community organizations that deliver critical community services, including housing and utility assistance, food access, health care and more. Funding will help modernize technology, expand food distribution networks, improve case management systems, coordinate volunteers and enhance fundraising and service delivery capabilities.

Senior Vibrancy: $500,000 will support 22 community organizations serving older North Carolinians through home repairs, meal programs, transportation assistance, benefits navigation, emergency financial support and other services that help seniors live independently, safely and with dignity.

Why it matters: “Duke Energy Foundation’s work is rooted in a simple belief: when our customers and communities need support, we must show up in meaningful, practical ways,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy’s North Carolina president. “We know families and seniors across our state are making careful decisions about household expenses, especially during summer when energy use can increase. These grants help trusted nonprofits meet people where they are – with food, housing support, home repairs, health resources and the local care that keeps communities strong.”

Positive response:

Ashley McCumber, executive director of Meals on Wheels of Wake County: “We’re honored to partner with the Duke Energy Foundation in supporting older adults across Wake County. This generous grant strengthens our ability to combat senior hunger and social isolation – two challenges that often go hand in hand. By investing in Meals on Wheels and our 10 Friendship Cafes across the county, Duke Energy Foundation is helping older adults stay healthy, connected and independently living in their own home while building a stronger, more compassionate community for every generation.”

Cindy Stubblefield, director of philanthropy for Habitat for Humanity of Forsyth County: “Thanks to Duke Energy’s support of our Home Repair Program, Habitat for Humanity of Forsyth County will be able to make much needed repairs and improvements for senior adults who otherwise could not afford to make them. Improvements such as the replacement of aging roofs and HVAC systems, and aging-in-place modifications like walk-in showers and grab bars, make all the difference in whether seniors are able to remain safely and comfortably in their own homes.”

Jordyn Appel-Hughes, executive director of Feast Down East: “Through our Mobile Farmers’ Market program, we see that many of the seniors living in our community across the region struggle to access healthy foods at affordable prices. With the money from the Duke Energy Foundation, we will be able to further support our senior communities through our Senior Mobile Market Voucher Program, which will reduce the cost burden that many seniors face when food shopping.”

A decade of investment: Connecting customers with resources that help ease financial pressure and improve quality of life has been a longstanding priority for Duke Energy. Since 2016, Duke Energy and its Foundation have invested:

More than $34.6 million to support nonprofit programs that help North Carolinians meet essential needs, including food access, housing stability, health services, transportation, senior support and emergency financial assistance

More than $31 million in Share the Light Fund and Share the Warmth agencies, helping customers facing financial hardship pay energy bills and maintain utility service

One step further: Financial support is paired with hands-on service. Duke Energy employees are rolling up their sleeves with organizations like Crisis Assistance Ministry and Oak City Cares to help expand the reach and impact of programs that serve their communities.

Since 2016, Duke Energy employees have volunteered more than 37,300 hours in North Carolina with organizations addressing community needs.

Tools to manage energy use and pay your way: In addition to financial assistance, Duke Energy offers more than a dozen tools and resources to help customers manage energy use during the summer months when cooling systems work harder, including:

Usage Alerts to track electricity use and cost before the bill arrives

Free home energy assessments, where professionals provide an energy efficiency kit, customized energy usage report and expert recommendations to save energy and money

Payment plans and due date extensions for customers needing flexibility

To learn more about these programs, visit duke-energy.com/SummerSolutions.

How you can help: Join Duke Energy in supporting neighbors in need through Share the Light Fund. Customers can make one-time or recurring donations – including through monthly bill round-up programs – with contributions matched by Duke Energy and the Duke Energy Foundation.

Duke Energy Foundation

The Duke Energy Foundation provides more than $30 million annually in philanthropic support to meet the needs of communities where Duke Energy customers live and work. The Foundation is funded by Duke Energy shareholders.

Duke Energy

Duke Energy (NYSE: DUK), a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., is one of America’s largest energy holding companies.
