text:
The U.S. electric car market in 2026 has entered a notable cooling phase, marked by a stabilization of new EV market share at roughly six percent. According to Cox Automotive's analysis, this is a significant downswing compared to its 10.6 percent peak in late 2025. This deceleration in mainstream consumer demand stems from several colliding factors, most notably the sunsetting of federal clean vehicle tax credits, persistent gaps in public charging infrastructure, and a broader consumer pivot toward conventional hybrids.

Furthermore, strict regulatory battery sourcing mandates and rising production tariffs have kept initial manufacturer costs high. Despite these headwinds, EVs remain an exceptionally compelling option for premium buyers who prioritize ultimate energy efficiency. Because automakers have significantly improved thermal management and aerodynamics, real-world highway range and fast-charging capabilities are better than ever. For those willing to absorb the higher upfront MSRPs, the combination of unmatched thermal efficiency, reduced operating and maintenance costs, and a progressively smoother daily driving experience still provides an excellent long-term ownership proposition.

Common Issues Currently Affecting EV Ownership

While first-year ownership satisfaction has actually hit record highs for those who embrace the technology, American electric vehicle owners still voice a distinct set of grievances regarding daily usability. The most widespread complaints center around software and electronic glitches. New EV owners frequently report troublesome infotainment setups, failed over-the-air updates, and laggy smartphone apps that fail to maintain a reliable connection to the vehicle. Additionally, despite notable expansions in public charging access, infrastructure anxiety remains a core frustration.

There remains a common issue of broken public chargers, confusing payment interfaces, and sluggish charging speeds that fail to meet advertised peak rates. Finally, practical and climate-related limitations continue to trigger buyer's remorse. Drivers in colder regions face severe winter range degradation, sometimes losing up to 32 percent of their driving range in freezing temperatures. EV truck owners frequently complain that towing heavy loads cuts their battery range straight in half, severely compromising the utility of electric pickups.

Nissan's Pragmatic American EV Strategy

Nissan's approach to electrification in the U.S. targets sensible and value-oriented commuters. Tech-conscious suburban buyers looking for a straightforward, fuss-free transition away from internal combustion engines are also a key demographic. Its pricing strategy relies heavily on affordability, aiming to undercut premium competitors by positioning its electric lineup as accessible entry points into the EV segment. Nissan frequently takes advantage of aggressive regional leasing incentives to counteract the loss of some federal clean vehicle tax credits.

However, according to the company’s Q1 2026 U.S. sales report, this strategy has faced severe headwinds. While the brand’s conventional internal combustion SUVs and trucks saw healthy retail momentum, its electric vehicles performed exceptionally poorly, suffering a steep decline in volume as consumer interest sharply dropped. One of its primary, long-standing electric options plunged by over 70 percent year-over-year to just 668 examples, and its newer flagship electric crossover achieved a mere fraction of its prior-year volume.

Nissan's Intelligent New Take On The Leaf

The 2026 Nissan Leaf anchors the brand's electrification strategy as its foundational, high-volume entry point, filling a vital slot just below the larger Ariya SUV. Fully redesigned for 2026, the model shifts from its traditional compact hatchback shape into an aerodynamically optimized subcompact crossover. This signals a modern and highly competitive approach to budget-friendly electric mobility. With a starting MSRP of just under $30,000 for the base trim, it aggressively addresses modern entry-level electrification by serving as one of the most affordable brand-new EVs available in the U.S.

Nissan pairs this value with crucial, contemporary upgrades, including a liquid-cooled battery pack for vastly superior winter thermal management, drastically increased driving range, and native compatibility with the North American Charging Standard. For Nissan, the Leaf acts as a defensive volume play designed to retain loyal, budget-conscious buyers and attract first-time EV adopters at a time when rising segment prices risk alienating mainstream consumers.

Performance Remains Accessible And Modest

The front-wheel-drive powertrain of the 2026 Nissan Leaf features a permanent-magnet synchronous electric motor that generates 214 horsepower and 261 pound-feet of torque. This is able to achieve a 0 to 60 MPH acceleration time of 6.9 seconds before hitting an electronically governed top speed of 102 MPH.

Nissan does not recommend towing with the Leaf. While the rear subframe can support aftermarket bolt-on receivers for lightweight bike racks or cargo trays, the factory warranty does not cover trailer towing.

Great Energy Consumption Estimates

The 2026 Nissan Leaf is available with three wheel options, all of which yield different energy consumption estimates. Based on the EPA's testing, Leaf models with the base 18-inch steel wheels return a combined 28 kWh per 100 miles and 303 miles of range on a single charge. Your annual electricity cost likely comes in at $650. Upgrading to 18-inch alloys worsens consumption to 30 kWh per 100 miles and cuts range to 288 miles. This will add $50 to your annual charging budget. The flagship's 19-inch wheel increases consumption to 33 kWh per 100 miles and reduces range to 259 miles. This will cost $750 to keep charged throughout the year.

The Leaf's Troublesome Market Launch

The 2026 Nissan Leaf is a new take on the brand's hallmark budget EV, but it hasn't been the best reboot. J.D. Power gives the newcomer a respectable 72/100 consumer-verified overall score, including 76/100 for quality and reliability and 85/100 for the dealership experience. Unfortunately, it only gets 57/100 for the driving experience and 67/100 for resale.

iSeeCars gives the Leaf a 7/10 score for reliability, indicating that it will cover an average lifespan of just nine years or 69,862 miles. In terms of value retention, the publication suggests that it will lose $17,706 or 62.9 percent of its value after five years of ownership. Being a niche newcomer, the 2026 Leaf only has three review submissions on the Edmunds consumer review portal, resulting in a 4.3/5 overall score. Key strengths include its visual presence, driving experience, and interior, but there have been some concerns regarding build quality.

Three Well-Balanced Trims

The entry-level S+, priced at $29,990, serves as the modern tech-forward baseline for the lineup, focusing heavily on digital real estate and seamless connectivity. The dashboard plays host to a pair of 12.3-inch widescreen displays. One acts as a configurable instrument cluster and the other as a highly responsive infotainment touchscreen. The system includes standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto integration, two front USB-C ports, and a standard four-speaker audio system. In terms of comfort and convenience, the S+ comes equipped with an energy-efficient cabin heat pump to preserve winter range, cloth-trimmed six-way manually adjustable front seats, automatic climate control with rear foot ducting, and the convenience of ProPILOT Assist alongside an approach-unlock and walk-away auto-locking keyless entry system.

Stepping up to the mid-tier SV+ trim costs $34,230, but adds the benefit of a more premium and connected cabin ambiance. The digital landscape expands via dual 14.3-inch widescreen displays that feature Google built-in, natively integrating Google Maps, Google Assistant, and Google Play directly into the vehicle’s ecosystem. Charging convenience is upgraded with a front wireless phone charging pad and the addition of two rear charge-only USB-C ports, while the audio experience expands to a clearer six-speaker layout. Comfort sees a major lift with the introduction of heated TailorFit synthetic leather front seats, a leather-wrapped steering wheel, a sunglasses holder, and steering-wheel-mounted regenerative braking paddles that give the driver manual control over energy recuperation.

The range-topping Platinum+ trim for $38,990 delivers a more luxurious experience. The defining interior centerpiece is a segment-first electrically dimming panoramic roof that alters its transparency from clear to near-opaque at the touch of a button, entirely eliminating the need for a physical sunshade. There's also a class-exclusive 10-speaker Bose Personal Plus Audio System, which features innovative speakers embedded into the front headrests to isolate navigation instructions or phone calls directly to the driver. The luxury treatment is rounded out by TailorFit upholstery across both the front and rear rows, heated rear seats, a heated steering wheel, automatic rain-sensing windshield wipers, customizable 64-color ambient interior lighting, and two household 120-volt power outlets capable of delivering up to 1,500 watts of Vehicle-to-Load electricity for external devices.

text:
Berlin — German luxury carmaker Porsche AG will cut around one in five jobs by 2035, with 9,000 positions to be axed in total, as parent Volkswagen AG and its brands restructure in the face of weak demand and stiff competition.

In a deal announced on Monday after months of negotiations, Porsche management and labor representatives agreed to 5,000 additional job cuts that avoid compulsory redundancies through measures like natural attrition and voluntary schemes.

These measures follow a first package of 3,900 job cuts agreed in February 2025 and another 500 announced by CEO Michael Leiters this year linked to the closure of subsidiaries.

Porsche had a workforce of some 42,600 at the end of 2024.

On becoming CEO at the start of the year, Leiters was tasked with overhauling the business after sales in Porsche's once highly lucrative China market collapsed and its EV strategy stalled.

The job cuts roughly correspond to the decline in sales volume, said Daniel Schwarz, automotive analyst at investment bank Metzler. "They are unavoidable in order to reduce costs, because a return to strong growth in China is not expected," he said.

Other German carmakers including Mercedes-Benz AG and BMW AG are also cutting costs as they navigate the shift to electric vehicles in a race with Chinese rivals while absorbing the impact of high tariffs.

The deal announced by Porsche also includes guarantees to keep sites open for another five years, until the end of 2035, as well as €2.1 billion ($2.39 billion) in investments in its main factory of Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen and its R&D centre in Weissach, the company and the works council said in a statement.

The announcement followed a meeting of Porsche's supervisory board last Wednesday, in which the committee gave its blessing to the additional cuts.

Leiters' predecessor Oliver Blume remains CEO of Volkswagen, having ended a dual leadership role that was opposed by many investors.

Blume is now pushing for a doubling of job cuts across the Volkswagen group to 100,000, measures that he says are necessary to remain competitive as more Chinese brands come to Europe.

He has also warned that four of the group's factories, including one belonging to premium brand Audi, are threatened with closure after 2030.

title: Attorney General calls on Duke Energy to commit to data center protections for ratepayers
description:
Duke Energy has joined the federal Ratepayer Protection Pledge — a promise to reduce the impact of data centers on electricity costs.
The Ratepayer Protection Pledge contains language committing tech companies to buy new power, or bring their own, for data center operation.
In this guidance, the utility commits to conduct engineering studies ensuring data center grid reliability and sign long-term agreements with large energy customers ensuring responsible growth.
Data centers can use as much energy as a small town – and utilities have been scrambling to accommodate them.
Across North Carolina and the country, concerns about the environmental and energy impact of data centers have repeatedly crossed party lines.
text:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between BPR and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.

Duke Energy has joined the federal Ratepayer Protection Pledge — a promise to reduce the impact of data centers on electricity costs. Now, North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson is calling on the utility to commit in a more concrete, legally binding manner, by agreeing to a new tariff through the North Carolina Utilities Commission.

The Trump administration first unveiled this federal pledge in March, after seven major tech companies, like Microsoft and Google, signed on. On Thursday, President Trump held a press conference touting the pledge’s expansion, saying 200 governors, legislators, developers, and power providers, including Duke and the Tennessee Valley Authority, had also signed the pledge.

The Ratepayer Protection Pledge contains language committing tech companies to buy new power, or bring their own, for data center operation. It also asks them to invest in the local workforce, create voluntary energy agreements for new rate structures with local utilities, and contribute to enhancing grid reliability and new power infrastructure.

Duke also recently announced its Customer Protection Plus framework, which is the utility’s own pledge. In this guidance, the utility commits to conduct engineering studies ensuring data center grid reliability and sign long-term agreements with large energy customers ensuring responsible growth.

Attorney General Jeff Jackson told BPR that while the pledge is encouraging, it’s not legally binding until Duke signs an agreement with the state utilities commission to keep costs from being borne by energy customers.

“So now the question is, did Duke do that just to please the federal administration or are they serious about it?” Jackson asked. “Are they willing to join us and actually put it in writing to the Utilities Commission and say we hereby agree to do this and protect the costs, make sure they're not shifted onto families?”

Jackson wants the utility to institute a large load tariff, requiring large energy customers like data centers to cover the costs of their electricity generation and infrastructure. Data centers can use as much energy as a small town – and utilities have been scrambling to accommodate them.

Duke initially sought an 18% rate increase this year, projecting increased electric load growth coming from both population and data center demand on the grid. The state objected, and Duke reached a proposed settlement with the N.C. Utilities Commission that cut the request nearly in half to 9.5%.

Duke spokesperson Jeffrey Brooks told BPR that while Duke’s current share of the load is about 1%, he expects that share to grow by 13% over the next few years. The utility is having conversations about tariffs, he said, but believes the Consumer Protection Pledge proves the utility is invested in keeping rates low.

“Our analysis shows us that large load customers, like data centers, will not only pay for the costs required to serve them, but they will also contribute additional revenue to help keep costs lower for other customers as well, and that's going to remain the case regardless of whether a large load tariff is established or not,” Brooks said.

Across North Carolina and the country, concerns about the environmental and energy impact of data centers have repeatedly crossed party lines. Communities are left uncertain and fearful of the AI-driven rapid rise in hyperscaler construction, and resulting impacts, including visual blight on the landscape, water use, energy rates, and air pollution, even as communities currently hosting hyperscale data centers feel left out of the companies’ decision making.

text:
As megawatt-level charging hubs for heavy-duty EVs proliferate around Europe, Portuguese EV charging infrastructure provider i-charging has begun commercial deliveries of its new MAX charging platform.

The MAX platform is built around SOLUM’s EV Power Module. Founded in 2015 as a spin-off from Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SOLUM develops power electronics for megawatt charging applications.

i-charging’s MAX platform scales from 50 kW to 1.6 MW within a single cabinet, and supports CCS, NACS, China’s GB/T standard and the new Megawatt Charging System (MCS). i-charging’s dynamic power allocation technology distributes available power in real time across up to eight simultaneously connected vehicles. Power allocation automatically adapts to each vehicle’s charging demand.

At the core of the platform is SOLUM’s EV Power Module. Designed to operate with up to 32 modules in parallel, the system enables megawatt-class charging within a compact footprint.

Following the first installations in Portugal, the companies plan to expand deployment of the MAX platform into additional European markets. Orders have already been received from Germany and Switzerland.

“Bringing a 1.6 MW charging system from product announcement to commercial installation is a significantly greater challenge than much of the industry assumed for a long time,” said Pedro Silva, CEO of i-charging. “In addition to technical specifications, the ability to scale at the pace demanded by European public charging operators and fleet operators is equally important.”

“This first commercial delivery demonstrates that SOLUM’s EV Power Module can serve as the heart of megawatt-scale charging systems,” said Daniel Lee, CEO of SOLUM Europe. “As we begin deliveries across Europe together with i-charging, our focus is on ensuring that every installed megawatt creates value for fleet and logistics operators driving electrification in Portugal and across Europe.”

title: Ohio's cautionary tale on data centers is a lesson for us all - The Hill
authors: Cathy Cowan Becker, opinion contributor, Cathy Cowan Becker, opinion contributor
description:
But that’s what happened, thanks to a new law allowing data centers to fast-track approval for “behind-the-meter” energy generation.
More than 50 communities have passed data center moratoriums, and a statewide volunteer group is collecting signatures for a ballot initiative that would ban data centers over 25 MW.
The Buckeye State ranks fifth for data centers, with 240 statewide.
If your county or state is not yet building fracked gas to power data centers, you can still reach out to legislators and demand renewable energy and guardrails for data centers.
There is a wrong way to power data centers, but you can push your state to do it right.
text:
When I moved to the thriving suburb of Hilliard, Ohio, three years ago, I never imagined I would be on the front lines of fossil fuel expansion. But that’s what happened, thanks to a new law allowing data centers to fast-track approval for “behind-the-meter” energy generation.

That law makes Ohio a case study on how not to power a data center.

Starting in 2020, Hilliard welcomed three Amazon data center campuses. The projects were seen as major investments bringing in good-paying jobs and tax revenue for schools. But in 2025, the Ohio legislature passed House Bill 15, which allows data centers to get approval for “major utility facilities” on land they own to generate energy behind the meter — meaning the electricity is not put onto the grid but used solely to power the data center.

The process takes just 60 days, with no public notice, no public hearing and no consultation with local officials. Approval is automatic, meaning no formal vote. And because the generation facility must go on land owned by the data center, the only viable option is gas.

Soon after H.B. 15 went into effect, and before anyone knew what was happening, the largest fracked-gas fuel cell project in North America was quietly approved, and an air permit issued for one of Hilliard’s Amazon data centers. The gas fuel cell will emit 1.45 million pounds of carbon dioxide every day — as if 66,000 gas cars were parked onsite and running 24/7 — next to hundreds of homes, a park and an elementary school.

Hilliard is just one example of behind-the-meter gas generation for data centers in Ohio. So far, 11 combustion gas turbine plants totaling 5,200 MW have been proposed or approved to power data centers across the state.

Others include:

The Socrates North and Socrates South gas plants, totaling 400 MW, were approved to power Meta’s Prometheus complex in New Albany, the world’s first gigawatt data center. Additional power will come from deals for three offsite nuclear projects.

The 350 MW Apollo gas plant got fast-track approval to power a Meta data center in Wood County with no public hearing. A shell company, Liames LLC, signed non-disclosure agreements with elected officials, hiding the project for months.

EdgeConneX has proposed an 800 MW gas project to power a data center complex in the tiny village of Ashville. The village council signed an agreement to support the gas plant, located next to children’s soccer fields and on top of the village aquifer, after the company offered $102 million for schools and critical wastewater upgrades.

Four gas plants totaling 1150 MW — Socrates North, Socrates South, Socrates the Younger and NEO Power Generation Facility — have been approved and proposed to power Meta’s Prometheus complex in New Albany, the world’s first gigawatt data center.

Vantage seeks to build a 1,350 MW gas plant with 40 turbines just a mile from the resort town of Millersport. Diagrams show particulate pollution would cover the village, Buckeye Lake State Park, and Cranberry Bog Nature Preserve, the only floating sphagnum moss island in the world. The project got a $76.1 million state tax break.

Meanwhile, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick unveiled plans for a 9.2 gigawatt — that’s 9200 megawatts — gas plant to power a giant data center complex in Pike County on the former site of the Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant, which enriched uranium for atomic weapons during the Cold War. Financed by $33 billion from Japan’s SoftBank, it would be the largest gas project in the world, spewing more than 53 million tons of greenhouse gas pollution each year.

Together all these gas projects will create more greenhouse pollution than many entire countries.

So many gas plants will surely carry a great cost for people and the environment. A study by Harvard biostatistician Michael Cork found that a 96 MW gas plant with eight turbines to power a Vantage data center in Loudon County, Va., could result in $53 million to $99 million in health damages, in addition to 3.4 to 6.5 additional deaths per year due to asthma, hospitalizations and lost productivity. Most gas plants now being built are much larger.

The prospect of so many new gas plants has fueled a rush to frack Ohio’s public lands, with almost 22,000 acres of the state’s parks and wildlife areas approved for extraction.

This enormous demand for energy is now fueling a citizen backlash against data centers in Ohio. More than 50 communities have passed data center moratoriums, and a statewide volunteer group is collecting signatures for a ballot initiative that would ban data centers over 25 MW.

The Buckeye State ranks fifth for data centers, with 240 statewide. That puts Ohio on the front lines of fossil fuel expansion — but it doesn’t have to be this way. If your county or state is not yet building fracked gas to power data centers, you can still reach out to legislators and demand renewable energy and guardrails for data centers.

With the right laws and incentives, data centers can transform from an extractive burden to an engine that builds communities and the clean energy economy. There is a wrong way to power data centers, but you can push your state to do it right.

Cathy Cowan Becker is Responsible Finance Campaign Director at Green America and board president of Save Ohio Parks. She lives in Hilliard, Ohio.

text:
Mack Trucks and Volvo Trucks both announced Monday the rollout of updates to diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) inducement software in their portfolio of all post-2010 models to meet new Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidance.

The announcements from the Volvo Group brands follows similar announcements by Daimler Truck North America, Cummins and Paccar.

Under new EPA guidance, inducement speeds have been increased from 5 miles per hour to 25 miles per hour and increase the repair window from four hours up to 160 hours. Volvo and Mack say their software updates align with current EPA guidance related to selective catalytic reduction (SCR) systems and DEF-related inducement strategies.

The updated software is designed to provide customers with a practical and streamlined path to compliance while supporting reliable vehicle operation, the companies state.

[RELATED: What ‘Freedom to Fix’ means, how the 2027 NOx rule is (and isn’t) changing and more]

Mack updates began in spring

Mack reports it began incorporating the updated software in May 2026 on Mack Pioneer and all-new Mack Anthem models equipped with the Mack MP 13 engines and will have software updates available for all 2024 and newer vehicles by the end of the summer.

Mack states it also is broadening availability of changes outlined in the EPA guidance document to include all post-2014 vehicles by the second quarter of 2027. By the end of 2027, owners of all eligible post-2010 vehicles that do not have remote software update capability will be able to receive the updated software through Mack dealers, the company says.

“Providing customers with practical solutions that support both compliance and operational efficiency remains a priority for Mack,” says Jonathan Randall, president of Mack Trucks North America. “By introducing this capability on new vehicles and establishing a clear path for legacy vehicle updates, we are helping customers maintain productivity while meeting evolving regulatory requirements.”

[RELATED: Not all stakeholders onboard with EPA’s DEF derate rules, warranty easement]

Volvo announces similar plans

At Volvo, all new trucks rolling off assembly lines now include updated DEF inducement software. In addition to new production vehicles, Volvo Trucks also is rolling out the updated software across in-service truck models, with availability continuing to expand throughout 2027. The updated software gives customers substantially more time to address DEF-related issues before the engine derates or the vehicle goes into reduced speed inducement, helping keep trucks moving and supporting the uptime customers depend on, the company says.

Additionally, since May 2026, Volvo Trucks has been producing D13 VGT and D13 TC engines featuring the updated software in the all-new VNL and all-new VNR trucks. The company says this updated software has been available in the aftermarket and has already been remotely downloaded into a large population of the new Volvo truck models. Volvo Trucks will roll out remote software updates to legacy Model Year 2024 and newer vehicles by the end of the summer.

Finally, Volvo Trucks also is broadening availability of changes outlined in the EPA guidance document to include all post-2014 model year vehicles by the second quarter of 2027 and all eligible post-2010 model year vehicles by the end of 2027. Truck models that do not have remote software update capability will be offered the updated software at their local Volvo Trucks dealerships.

“These updates are about giving our customers more flexibility and confidence when they are on the road,” says Peter Voorhoeve, president at Volvo Trucks North America. “By extending the repair window and increasing the final inducement speed, we are helping drivers keep their trucks on the road and safely reach a service location, reducing the risk of unexpected downtime and supporting the uptime and productivity our customers depend on every day.”

text:
Researchers have created a wearable patch that can detect hazards in the environment – such as dangerous gases or heavy metals in water – and then notify wearers by vibrating against their skin. The researchers have also extended the work to create an “e-skin” for robotic devices, allowing robots to detect and avoid hazards in their environment.

“There are already sensors that can detect environmental hazards and send notifications to your phone – we wanted to improve on that,” says Erim Uzunoğlu, first author of a paper on the work and a Ph.D. student at North Carolina State University. “We had two goals for this work. First, we wanted to miniaturize the sensors and incorporate them into a wearable patch to identify any potential risks to the wearer.

“Second, if you’re coming into contact with a hazardous substance, you need to know as quickly as possible. And if the notification is being sent to your phone, you may not check it right away. So we wanted to incorporate haptic technology into the patch so that it would vibrate as soon as the hazard was detected, allowing people to respond quickly to the potential threat.”

For this work, the researchers created a square patch slightly smaller than a driver’s license. The patch contains a microcontroller that serves as the patch’s brain; a very small battery; sensors to monitor for six environmental hazards; and a tiny actuator, which serves as the haptic motor that vibrates against the skin. The exterior of the patch also incorporates an array of thin-film photovoltaic cells, which allows the device to harvest solar power while being worn.

“Just having a buzzing motor isn’t enough; you need to actually feel it,” says Oluwatobi Ojuade, co-author of the paper and a Ph.D. student at NC State. “So, we designed tiny textured surfaces that sit at the interface between the motor and your skin, almost like a miniature pattern of bumps. By changing the size and spacing of those bumps, we could control how the vibration is perceived against your skin. That let us fine-tune the sensation so it actually grabs your attention, instead of feeling like a faint buzz you might miss.”

The device also triggers a different “haptic sequence,” or vibration pattern, for each hazard it detects. This allows wearers to determine which environmental hazard they need to be aware of.

“In proof-of-concept testing, we found that the device did a good job of detecting the hazardous substances and immediately triggering the haptic response,” says Uzunoğlu. “We also found the energy harvesting technology did a good job of extending the life of the battery. Coupled with the low power demand of the sensors, this allows the device to function for around 24 hours.”

As the researchers were developing the patch, they wondered whether it would be possible to extend the concept for use in robotic devices, allowing robots to detect and respond to hazards in their environment. That led to the development of what they call the e-skin.

The e-skin essentially layers the sensor patch over a layer of piezoelectric material. When the sensor detects a hazard and triggers the haptic response, the resulting vibration against the piezoelectric layer creates an electrical signal that can be detected by the robot.

In proof-of-concept testing, the e-skin allowed quadrupedal robots to detect hazards and alter their routes to avoid those hazards.

“The patch and e-skin are largely made using off-the-shelf components, with very few custom-engineered elements,” says Amay Bandodkar, co-corresponding author of the paper and an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at NC State. “That should make it easier to scale up the technology moving forward. And the concept is extremely flexible – the sensor array is modular, so you can add or remove sensors that monitor for whichever hazards are most relevant to the application.

“It’s quite amazing to see that we can encode tactile signals into materials of different properties, something that has been very challenging to do in the past – especially in real-world situations where people would want to wear the device,” says Lilian Hsiao, co-corresponding author and an associate professor of chemical and biomolecular engineering at NC State. “To combine something that people would wear, along with sophisticated sensing capabilities and the ability to alert the user, is something we’ve been working on for a long time.”

More than 600 direct jobs are expected during the first phase.

AfDB Backs a €1.3 Billion First Phase

The approved €100 million loan will help finance a cathode-to-cell lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery gigafactory led by China’s Gotion High-Tech. Gotion Power Morocco is the local project company, while its parent is headquartered in Hefei and listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange.

That mobilisation will take place under the New African Financial Architecture for Development, an initiative intended to coordinate institutions and unlock larger pools of capital for African projects. During phase one, the facility will have capacity to produce 10 GWh of cells and packs annually for electric vehicles. The long-term development plan targets 100 GWh, which would significantly increase Morocco’s role in the global battery manufacturing market.

Morocco Deepens Its Electric-Vehicle Strategy

Jobs, Local Integration and Execution Risks

The first phase is expected to create more than 600 direct jobs and achieve a 70% local industrial integration rate. This target could support domestic suppliers, technical training and the transfer of advanced manufacturing capabilities if the project successfully builds a competitive local network.

The facility is also expected to rely primarily on renewable energy, according to the project’s development outline, aligning battery production with Morocco’s wider clean-energy ambitions.

However, large battery projects remain capital-intensive and exposed to construction delays, technology changes, raw-material price volatility and shifting demand in global electric-vehicle markets. text:
Power purchase agreement prices for solar projects in North America experienced a 4.8% quarter over quarter decline in the second quarter of 2026, marking the first quarterly price decrease for solar in two years. Meanwhile, wind power purchase agreement prices continued their upward trajectory, rising 5.5% over the same period, according to the latest Q2 2026 report from marketplace operator LevelTen Energy.

The quarterly report, which analyzed 266 price offers from 185 renewable energy projects across six Independent System Operators, presents a shifting landscape shaped by softening buy-side demand, federal permitting bottlenecks, and the impending expiration of clean energy tax credits.

Market averaged solar prices fell across North America during the second quarter, driven heavily by a steep price drop in the California Independent System Operator market. LevelTen noted that California accounted for more than half of the total continental decrease, and when excluding California, the continental average price drop moderated to 1.8%.

The decline reflects a broader softening in buy-side corporate demand. While technology giants and large data center operators continue to procure large volumes of clean energy, commercial and industrial buyers are exhibiting caution.

High contract costs and lingering uncertainty over proposed updates to the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Scope 2 accounting standards have led some corporate buyers to pause or slow procurement strategies. In response, project developers are sharpening contract terms to remain competitive in what is becoming a more buyer favorable environment.

In contrast to solar, wind power purchase agreement prices on the market averaged continental index climbed 5.5% quarter over quarter and are up 17.5% year over year.

Upward price momentum continues to be fueled by high fuel prices, elevated logistics costs, and persistent federal permitting friction. A major factor constraining new wind capacity is the Department of Defense’s near total halt on issuing national security mitigation agreements, which has been in place since August 2025. The resulting bottleneck has severely restricted the pipeline of new, buildable wind assets, forcing buyers to pay a premium for fully permitted projects.

The report places heavy emphasis on a critical industry milestone: the July 4 cutoff date for tax credit qualification established under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. With the passing of this deadline, the pool of tax credit eligible projects in the United States will effectively freeze.

As tax subsidized capacity becomes increasingly scarce, LevelTen warns that overall power purchase agreement contract prices are likely to enter higher, uncharted territory. Furthermore, tax credit qualified projects must achieve commercial operation and be placed in service by the end of 2030 to maintain eligibility, creating added urgency for corporate buyers to finalize agreements and help developers reach financial close.

Despite surging contract prices up to 151% since 2020, LevelTen analysis indicates that corporate buyers who delayed procurement in hopes of lower prices faced estimated cost impacts of $32 million to $65 million per 200 MW project across major regional markets.

Despite market volatility, LevelTen said that virtual power purchase agreements remain one of the most effective tools for corporate buyers to hedge against power grid price spikes and macroeconomic risk. On the continental level, Q2 2026 price benchmarks averaged $61.40 per MWh for solar, $83.79 per MWh for wind, and $72.60 per MWh, with 25th percentile offer values standing at $52.65 dollars for solar and $61.19 dollars for wind.

text:
NEW YORK, NY – Today the New York Embodied Carbon Working Group, a coalition of diverse industry leaders and subject-matter experts, has released the New York Embodied Carbon Action Plan – a comprehensive set of recommendations and precedents to guide state regulators to develop a plan to reduce emissions from building and infrastructure construction. Over the next 25 years, more than half the emissions from new buildings will come from the materials themselves. As buildings become more efficient, the materials they’re made out of are coming under new focus.

A summary of New York State Embodied Carbon Action Plan recommendations includes:

1. Establish statewide embodied carbon reduction targets. Empower state agencies and industries to address the climate challenge by adopting a statutory reduction requirement statewide.

2. Set embodied carbon reduction requirements for buildings in codes. Establish a long-term strategy for reducing embodied carbon in public and private building projects by setting three compliance pathways for reducing embodied carbon in building or zoning codes.

3. Establish embodied carbon reduction requirements for state agencies’ infrastructure projects. Leverage the large portfolio of the 12 state agencies that oversee construction by requiring them to quantify and track embodied carbon emissions, as well as implementing Envision Certification requirements across relevant state agency projects.

4. Help manufacturers and suppliers develop low-carbon construction materials. Foster the innovative low-carbon market by implementing a low-carbon product standard, establishing a test center for low-carbon concrete and asphalt mixtures, creating an embodied carbon reduction challenge at the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA), and expanding financing and incentives available to manufacturers.

5. Incentivize the use of low-carbon construction materials. Financially support producers and users of low-carbon construction materials by providing sales tax exemptions for low-carbon materials, establishing an environmental product declaration (EPD) grant program, and expanding eligibility for the R&D Tax Credit.

6. Encourage localities to address embodied carbon. Provide resources and incentives to encourage localities to implement or pilot portions of state agency policies at the municipal or county levels.

7. Collaborate with industry to drive standardization in the marketplace. Collaborate with industry stakeholders across New York to help reduce embodied carbon by increasing capacity, addressing cost concerns, and coordinating with other efforts to minimize the duplication of efforts—saving the public money and reducing the time and monetary burden on private enterprise.

The following are quotes from supporters of the Action Plan:

“While the direct impacts of embodied carbon are not visible, the emissions generated from today’s new buildings and infrastructure will last far into the future. As State, County, and Municipal programs make strides in reducing the operational emissions associated with our buildings, these strategies will enable state entities to also reduce the emissions from materials, many of which are no or low cost when compared to standard options,” saidMikhail Haramati, State Industrial Lead, Climate & Energy at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council). “Innovation and project development for these building materials supports good-paying New York jobs.”

“As a participant in the development of the New York State Embodied Carbon Action Plan, the MTA is pleased to see the results of this collaborative effort. The MTA is proud to be a leader in reducing the carbon footprint of our construction materials, specifically our use of concrete, and always happy to lead by example in sustainable practices. All parties involved should be congratulated for their dedication to reducing emissions in New York State, and ultimately around the world,” said Thomas Abdallah, Vice President of Design Services and Chief Environmental Engineer at the Metropolitan Transportation Authority.

“New York has demonstrated that climate leadership is about more than reducing operational emissions—it also requires fundamental change in how we build and unbuild. By treating existing buildings as valuable material resources and supporting reuse at scale, this Action Plan charts a practical path to reducing embodied carbon while strengthening local economies and creating green jobs,” said Felix Heisel, Director of the Circular Construction Lab at Cornell University.

“These high-impact strategies, designed to curb embodied carbon and catalyze circular construction, are built upon a foundational economic framework that will revitalize regional commerce and empower New York State neighborhoods to flourish.” said Gretchen Worth, Project Director, Susan Christopherson Center for Community Planning

“The New York Embodied Carbon Action Plan provides a unified roadmap for all professionals who influence our physical surroundings. Our duty spans from the initial decision-making phase—prioritizing renovation and mindful construction—to the very selection of materials. Addressing both architecture and civil engineering, this initiative fulfills that obligation with reality-based tactics. Architecture 2030 is honored to stand with the partnership spearheading this effort,” said Vincent Martinez, CEO of Architecture 2030.

“In our collective fight to reduce the carbon emissions of the building sector, we need all hands on deck. This Embodied Carbon Action Plan for New York is an impressive result from an impressive collaboration that rightfully points towards the critical role of good policy to catalyze emissions reductions. This work promises to be useful beyond the State of New York with other states and municipalities who are seeking effective policies to hit their climate action goals. Congratulations to the partners and participants, and thank you,” said Lindsay Baker, CEO,International Living Future Institute.

"New York has enormous potential to build on the embodied carbon programs established over the past few years — turning what's often an untapped climate solution into real, measurable action. We're thrilled to see this action plan come to fruition with tangible recommendations across the built environment," said Anthony Hickling, Executive Director, Carbon Leadership Forum.

"The inclusion of Envision in the New York State Embodied Carbon Action Plan reflects the understanding that achieving net-zero carbon and delivering broader social and environmental benefits should go hand in hand,” said Anthony Kane, President & CEO, Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure.

“By implementing supportive policies to elevate building material reuse from a mere 1% to just 5%, we could divert 300,000 tons of perceived waste back into the local market as valuable resources. This shift would create 6,000 full-time positions and stimulate more than $2 billion in yearly economic activity across the state. Furthermore, it increases the availability of low-cost supplies, bolsters regional commerce, mitigates pollution, and curbs the carbon intensity of manufacturing by prolonging the utility of existing products,” said Brad Guy, Principal, Material Reuse.

Coalition Background: During the 2025 summer season, the New York Embodied Carbon Working Group was formed to address embodied carbon reduction projects in New York state, amid news of catastrophic cuts to federal programs and funding. A voluntary group, composed of practitioners and technical experts working on embodied carbon in the region, the group released its high-impact near-term recommendations for policy action in September 2025, along with a 10-year vision for New York state. The working group experts include architects, builders, engineers, public sector staff, policy professionals, consultants, contractors, academics, and industry associations.

For more information, visit: Cross-Sector Working Group Releases Embodied Carbon Action Plan for New York State.

text:
Download PDF

The United States Government Accountability Office (“GAO”) issued a July report titled:

Critical Minerals: Reducing U.S. Import Reliance with Substitution and Recycling Technologies (“Report”).

The Report is transmitted to the following:

The Honorable Gary Palmer, Chairman, Subcommittee on Environment Committee on Energy and Commerce, House of Representatives.

The Honorable John Joyce, M.D., Chairman, Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations Committee on Energy and Commerce, House of Representatives.

The above referenced Congressmen asked GAO to describe substitution and recycling technologies that are available for deployment in the near term (two to three years) that may reduce United States import reliance on critical minerals in the semiconductor and battery industries. As a result, GAO examined:

The state of and potential opportunities and impacts of these technologies to lessen import reliance on critical minerals within these industries,

Challenges to the development and adoption of these technologies, and

Policy options that could support the policy goal of reducing critical mineral import reliance.

GAO selected 11 critical minerals for examination based on their import reliance and importance to the battery and semiconductor industries.

It found by way of summary that substitution and recycling technologies could help reduce U.S. reliance on these imports. However, progress is stated to likely take many years in some cases.

The Report addressed:

Batteries (noting substitution and recycling technologies offer near-term potential to reduce cobalt, manganese, and nickel in the next 2 to 3 years, but such batteries do not perform as well in other applications, like long-haul electric vehicles, due to their lower energy density).

Semiconductors (most substitution and recycling technologies are likely years away from maturity, and unlikely to have a near-term effect on import reliance of minerals, such as gallium and indium, because other materials do not perform as well as these critical minerals across the same conditions).

Experts are stated to have informed GAO that industry will not adopt substitutes until they can perform at the same level as current semiconductor materials in the intended application.

Technologies to recycle minerals from semiconductors also face challenges, such as an underdeveloped market. However, semiconductor manufacturing scrap is referenced as a potential source of recycled minerals, though this is not yet standard practice in the U.S. Another potential source is discarded electronics, but the critical mineral content is low, and those minerals are generally mixed and bonded with other materials. Technologies to recycle this form of electronic waste are described as in pilot-stage development.

text:
Africa’s first EV battery gigafactory is nearing full production, as the African Development Bank Group (AfDB) approves a further US$113.7m investment.

Morocco will host the continent’s first EV battery facility, producing 10GWh of battery cells, anodes and cathodes.

More than 600 jobs are expected to be generated from the Moroccan plant and continue Africa’s transition to clean energy.

Africa’s first EV battery gigafactory

In May 2023, Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion High-Tech signed a memorandum of understanding with the Moroccan government to produce EV batteries in Africa.

Together, the two companies formed Gotion Power Morocco and accelerated lithium-ion battery technology production and energy storage systems in Africa.

By the end of 2024, an initial US$1.3bn investment was agreed and construction in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra Free Trade Zone began in May 2025.

According to the International Trade Council, plans could scale up over the coming years and reach a total investment of US$6.4bn.

Despite starting at 10GWh of battery cells and batteries for EVs per year, Gotion Power Morocco has set plans to increase production to 100GWh.

The facility will span 1.56 million m² and is expected to reach 6.35 million m² after its full construction.

Volkswagen Group holds a 33% stake in Gotion, which could strengthen the Moroccan supply chain to European automotive manufacturers.

Kevin Kariuki, the Bank Group’s Vice President for Power, Energy, Climate and Green Growth, says: “Battery storage is the missing link in Africa's clean energy transition. A facility of this scale, powered primarily by renewable energy, strengthens the foundations for the large-scale integration of solar and wind power, which our grids increasingly depend on.”

Why is it in Morocco?

The African nation is just 14km from Spain and has traded with European nations for decades through the Tanger Med Port.

Sitting in Northern Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, Tanger Med Port is Africa’s largest container port, handling 10,241,392 containers in 2024, according to Tanger Med Port Authority.

It is the second largest trade gateway globally and boasts connectivity to 180 ports and 70 countries.

Alongside its favourable location, Morocco also has trade agreements with key manufacturing countries across the world.

It is the only African nation that holds a comprehensive Free Trade Agreement with the US, a deal that has been running since 2004.

Morocco has also built a strong trade relationship with the European Union since the EU-Morocco Association Agreement was signed in 1996.

In the AfDB’s 2025 Africa Industrialisation Index, Morocco was top of the rankings, dethroning South Africa, which held pole position for 15 years.

text:
Washington, DC -- With temperatures spiking across the country this summer, top American cities are no longer waiting for the federal government to save them. They are using their own resources, plus partnerships with innovative non-profits, to drive down the sweltering heat in metropolitan areas.

Already, 11 major US cities including Atlanta, Boston, Charlotte, Dallas, New Orleans, Phoenix, Portland and many others are adopting “smart surfaces” to lower the heat in dense urban areas burdened by dark, impervious surfaces including roofs, roads, and parking lots. The use of smart surfaces -- reflective roofs and roads, permeable pavements, green stormwater infrastructure, and shade trees -- can reduce peak summer air temperatures by up to 7°F or more in hot neighborhoods. These smart surfaces also dramatically cut electricity bills and improve human health.

“We’re cooking our cities. They’re getting so hot every summer, it’s like we’ve turned the broiler to high. We’re making it increasingly dangerous for kids, the elderly, and other vulnerable populations,” says Greg Kats, CEO of the non-profit Smart Surfaces Coalition, which has partnered with the 11 US cities and surrounding metro areas. “But we can easily lower the heat, and cut electricity bills, by installing cool roofs and other smart surfaces that reflect a majority of solar heat.”

Kats and his team have detailed satellite maps that analyze heat, neighborhood by neighborhood, to show the cooling potential of reflective roofs and other smart surfaces in the 11 cities versus leafy suburban and rural areas. “As the Trump Administration has raced to eliminate climate funding and solutions across the US, major American cities are stepping up,” Kats said. In addition to the 11 cities already working on smart surfaces solutions, another 20 US cities and counties have signed letters of interest to do the same.

Across the 11 cities -- home to more than 9 million people -- citywide adoption of Smart Surfaces can deliver $7.6 billion in public health benefits, $3.3 billion in electricity bill reductions, and $9.9 billion in infrastructure savings, while also reducing or offsetting 79 million metric tons of CO₂e and managing 275 billion gallons of stormwater, Kats said.

"Designing healthier cities is paramount in the reality of our rapidly warming world. Outdated, heat-trapping surfaces put millions at risk -- especially in underserved neighborhoods,” added Georges C. Benjamin, MD, Executive Director of the American Public Health Association. “The Smart Surfaces Coalition’s new tools give cities the power to design healthier, cooler, and more resilient communities.”

title: EU Drafts a Plan to Double its Electrification and Limit Oil and Natural Gas - IER
description:
The Electrification Action Plan is part of the EU’s response to the Iran War, which raised oil and gas prices, prompting the EU to turn to new measures to cut Europe’s reliance on imported oil and gas.
Today, 23% of the EU’s energy consumption is met by electricity — a share that has been steady for a decade.
About 70% of EU electricity generation comes from renewables and nuclear.
The EU plan includes policies and funding to incentivize the transition to greater electrification, including tackling long grid connection times and helping new technologies reach commercial scale.
The EU imports more than 80% of the natural gas it consumes, and more than 90% of its oil.
text:
The European Union (EU) wants to increase its electricity use and is setting a goal of 46% of energy consumption across the bloc by 2040, doubling the rate today, following the direction of the World Economic Forum. The Electrification Action Plan is part of the EU’s response to the Iran War, which raised oil and gas prices, prompting the EU to turn to new measures to cut Europe’s reliance on imported oil and gas. Today, 23% of the EU’s energy consumption is met by electricity — a share that has been steady for a decade. The rest of the economy runs mostly on fossil fuels, and imports dominate those supplies due to European policies such as banning hydraulic fracturing and cutting offshore leasing. About 70% of EU electricity generation comes from renewables and nuclear. The EU plan includes policies and funding to incentivize the transition to greater electrification, including tackling long grid connection times and helping new technologies reach commercial scale.

Raising the electrification share to 46% would require a massive increase in electric vehicles, more widespread replacement of gas boilers with heat pumps in homes, electrifying industrial processes, and extensive upgrades of Europe’s aging power grids, requiring hundreds of billions of euros in investments. For the plan to succeed, policymakers would need to lower Europe’s high electricity prices, which are already much higher than those in the United States and have been leading to deindustrialization in Europe. Even then, for some firms it would not be economically feasible to electrify their operations.

According to the draft plan, achieving a 46% electrification target could reduce the EU’s fossil fuel import bill by up to €260 billion ($297 billion) per year by 2040. The EU imports more than 80% of the natural gas it consumes, and more than 90% of its oil. The Commission estimates that hitting the target of 46% would cut oil demand by 40% and gas demand by 70%. Since the escalation of the Middle East conflict, the EU has spent more than €50 billion ($57 billion) extra on fossil fuel imports.

The plan focuses on the main barriers identified by the Commission: the gap between electricity and gas prices; access to infrastructure; innovation; and the upfront cost of electrification technologies such as heat pumps and electric vehicles. The energy package also includes new measures on network charges aimed at making electricity grids more efficient by encouraging consumers, producers and grid operators to adapt their behavior. The initiative calls on member states to ensure electricity is not taxed more heavily than gas, arguing that taxation remains a barrier to electrification. However, the proposal stops short of dictating how countries set electricity tariffs. Instead, it establishes principles for national regulators to encourage smarter consumption, flexibility and more efficient grid management.

There is likely to be resistance from member states and challenges. The EU’s high consumer electricity-to-gas price ratios that compare the cost of a unit of electricity to a unit of natural gas per kilowatt hour are one challenge, as mentioned above. The EU electricity-to-gas price ratio currently exceeds 3.0, which is above the bloc’s targets of 2.5 for households and 2.0 for industry, mainly due to non-energy charges, levies, social tariffs and legacy subsidies.

According to the Commission’s Electrification Plan, “An energy transition with electrification at the forefront could, for example, support the business case for manufacturing electric vehicles in the EU by stimulating the uptake of approximately 120 million battery EVs compared to 8 million battery EVs today, and of approximately 100 million heat pumps compared to 30 million heat pumps installed today.” Around half of the EU’s gas consumption comes from buildings, which have been identified as one of the sectors with the greatest potential for electrification. On the other hand, buildings in Europe are not easily adapted to newer technologies, as demonstrated by low adoption of air conditioning. This is in part due to the age of the housing stock and intrinsic construction techniques.

The EU’s electrification rate of 23% is below those of China, Japan, and South Korea, which are closer to 30%, but is close to that of the United States and the world average.

As part of the new plan, the Commission intends to pursue a series of initiatives to support investment in electrification-related skills. These initiatives include adopting an initiative to support the portability of qualifications and skills across the EU to attract more electricians and clean technology installers, providing incentives for manufacturers to support training of electricians and installers under a new Clean Heat Market Mechanism, and for a new Construction Services Act that will make it easier to obtain certifications for energy-efficient building and installation work.

The Commission plans to assess whether to make the electrification rate binding as part of the post-2030 Energy Union package.

Conclusion

The EU wants to phase out fossil fuels and increase electrification, which means more electric vehicles, more heat pumps, and more electrification of industry. The Commission is targeting a 46% share of electricity by 2040, double its current share, which has been stagnant for the last decade. The EU sees this as relying on its own “clean” energy rather than on fossil fuels, which it mostly imports due to policies that ban hydraulic fracturing and cut offshore oil and gas leasing. Since the conflict in Iran began on February 28, the EU has spent $57 billion more on fossil fuels. An electrification target of 46% could reduce the EU’s fossil fuel import bill by up to €260 billion ($297 billion) per year by 2040 and cut oil demand by 40% and natural gas demand by 70%.

text:

GARY – The Gary Common Council unanimously approved a resolution urging U.S. Steel and its parent company, Nippon Steel, to invest in cleaner steelmaking technology at the Gary Works plant, saying modernization is essential to preserve jobs, strengthen the regional economy and reduce harmful pollution.

The resolution calls on the companies to use remaining investment funds committed to Gary Works to install a direct reduction iron facility and related equipment, replacing aging blast furnace technology with a process the council said produces fewer emissions while maintaining steel quality.

Council members also encouraged future steel manufacturing investments in Indiana.

In adopting the measure, the council cited Gary’s designation as an Environmental Protection Agency environmental justice community, noting residents have long faced industrial pollution and associated health concerns while also depending on the steel mill for jobs and tax revenue. The resolution argues that direct reduction technology would help improve air quality while keeping Gary Works competitive as the steel industry increasingly adopts newer production methods.

The council also urged U.S. Steel and Nippon Steel to comply with updated federal hazardous air pollution standards for integrated steel mills and pledged to work collaboratively on a transition that protects union jobs, supports workforce training and local hiring, and promotes long-term investment in Gary.

The resolution will be sent to state and federal officials, neighboring communities and other steel-producing regions.

title: Rivian R2 uses up to 26% more energy than Model Y in real-world test - Electrek
authors: Fred Lambert, Peter Johnson, Micah Toll
description:
Out of Spec Reviews put a Rivian R2 Performance and a Tesla Model Y Performance on the same roads on the same afternoon.
That’s awkward, because the two SUVs carry identical EPA efficiency ratings, and Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe has been telling media the R2 matches the Model Y.
The Model Y wins the highway cycle 100 to 96.
At 80 mph the R2 is a 2.2-to-2.5 mi/kWh vehicle and the Model Y is a 3.1-to-3.3 mi/kWh vehicle, and that’s not a rounding error.
And while the form factor is much less efficient than the Model Y, it’s also much more SUV, with an emphasis on utility, than Model Y.
text:
Out of Spec Reviews put a Rivian R2 Performance and a Tesla Model Y Performance on the same roads on the same afternoon. The R2 used 18% to 26% more energy at every single speed they tested.

That’s awkward, because the two SUVs carry identical EPA efficiency ratings, and Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe has been telling media the R2 matches the Model Y.

What the EPA numbers say

We covered the ratings when they landed in May: the R2 Performance matches the Model Y on EPA efficiency at 105 MPGe combined and 32 kWh per 100 miles. The R2 wins the city cycle 114 to 111. The Model Y wins the highway cycle 100 to 96. And the R2 goes further on a charge, 330 miles against 306.

For a vehicle that weighs roughly 800 lbs more and has the aerodynamic profile of a shoebox, that’s a real engineering achievement.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

Scaringe leaned into it at the R2 launch. Asked about the front drive unit disconnect, he told assembled media the R2 is “as efficient on a Wh per mile or miles per Wh basis despite the capabilities it has and despite the form factor that we’ve intentionally chosen to provide the level of utility that it has.”

But EPA ratings are lab numbers. And they rarely match real-world experience.

EPA lets automakers choose their own test

This part doesn’t get explained often enough, so here it is.

EPA gives EV manufacturers more than one path to a range and efficiency label. The cheap path: run the car on the city cycle until the battery is depleted, run it on the highway cycle until the battery is depleted, then multiply range and fuel economy by 0.7 to approximate real-world driving. EPA’s own guidance says most EVs use that method.

The expensive path is the multi-cycle test: four city cycles, two highway cycles, and two constant-speed cycles, which actually measures cold-weather, hot-weather and high-speed behavior instead of estimating it with a blanket factor. Automakers can also petition EPA for a derived five-cycle method or for adjustment factors based on in-use data. Both require EPA approval.

So a car that runs the longer, costlier test can earn a better correction factor than the flat 0.7. Out of Spec’s Kyle Conner believes that’s what happened here, with Rivian running the R2 through the full procedure at a lab in Michigan while Tesla submitted derived numbers. He says on camera that he can’t certify it, and neither can we. Per-vehicle test paths aren’t published anywhere the public can easily check them, which is its own problem.

There’s a second wrinkle nobody talks about. EPA’s kWh/100 miles figure is measured at the wall, so it includes charging losses. Out of Spec measured energy leaving the battery. Back the label math out and EPA is effectively saying the R2 does about 3.75 miles per kWh from the pack while the Model Y Performance does about 3.64 — EPA has the R2 slightly ahead, and testing put it 18% to 26% behind.

That gap is the whole story.

The side-by-side

Methodology first, because it’s the only thing that makes a comparison like this worth reading.

Both SUVs sat until the packs cooled to ambient. Tires set to 42 PSI cold with the same gauge. Climate on auto at 68°F with rear vents off, two occupants per vehicle, screens dimmed, no phone charging. R2 in Conserve, Model Y in Chill. Out-and-back loops at 50, 60, 70 and 80 mph GPS, with the cars swapping the lead each leg so neither one drafted. The two odometers disagreed by about 1.7%, so the comparison ran on kWh consumed rather than the cars’ own efficiency readouts.

Here’s how much more energy the R2 used at each speed, with its own efficiency in brackets:

50 mph: 18.4% more (4.00 mi/kWh)

60 mph: roughly 26% more (3.15 mi/kWh)

70 mph: roughly 20% more (3.06 mi/kWh)

80 mph: 26.5% more (2.46 mi/kWh)

The 70 mph result breaks the trend, and Conner explains why on camera: that loop ran on I-95 at 5 p.m. in heavy traffic, with both cars picking up slipstream from trucks. Treat it as the soft data point.

Then they built a low-speed city simulation, which is where Rivian’s argument should be strongest. The R2 decouples its front motor with a clutch, so crawling around town it spins one drive unit. The Model Y’s front induction motor keeps turning and paying windage and gear-train losses. Over a 20-minute stop-and-go loop the Model Y used 1.6 kWh and the R2 used 1.9, about 19% worse in the exact scenario built to favor it.

The charging is the good news

The second video ran Out of Spec’s 10% Challenge: charge from 10% state of charge for exactly 15 minutes, then drive at a constant 80 mph until you’re back to 10%.

The R2 charges well. Really well. Plugged into an IONNA Rechargery in Wilson, North Carolina, it held a flat 600 amps, everything the Alpitronic hardware could deliver, all the way to 32% state of charge, peaking around 229 kW. It added 48.3 kWh in 15 minutes for a 193 kW average, going from 10% to 59%. The car asks for up to 630 amps, meaning it was charger-limited rather than battery-limited for that entire window. For a 400-volt architecture, that’s about as good as it currently gets.

Then it drove 92.8 miles at 2.2 mi/kWh. The Model Y Performance, run two days earlier, managed roughly 103 miles at 3.3 mi/kWh on considerably less added energy, because it charges badly and cruises brilliantly.

Electrek’s Take

We wrote the May story off the EPA filings, and those filings said what they said. We’re not walking that back. What this testing exposes is a rating system that let two widely different vehicles land on the same combined number, and then a highway that reminded everyone shapes still matter.

One test day isn’t the last word, and we’d say that even if the result had gone the other way. Out of Spec used in-car energy meters instead of measuring at the charger, ran everything in summer heat on a single day, and had one of four loops compromised by traffic.

But directionally, this is what R2 owners are going to live with, because nobody actually drives the EPA city cycle. People drive 75 on the interstate. At 80 mph the R2 is a 2.2-to-2.5 mi/kWh vehicle and the Model Y is a 3.1-to-3.3 mi/kWh vehicle, and that’s not a rounding error. It makes sense based on the aerodynamic profiles of each vehicle.

The more useful framing is that Rivian made a trade, and it’s a defensible one. The R2 charges better than almost any 400-volt EV you can buy. And while the form factor is much less efficient than the Model Y, it’s also much more SUV, with an emphasis on utility, than Model Y.

We came away impressed by the R2 in our first drive, and this doesn’t change that, but it’s an important data point to consider if you are on the market for a R2. The efficiency figures from the EPA are likely inflated.

This would be a change for Rivian because in general, I found myself more likely to hit EPA efficiency in the R1s than in almost any Tesla vehicle I’ve driven.

description:
Despite a rocky year for EV sales in the U.S., BMW is taking a massive step forward by bringing battery production stateside.
Gallery: BMW Plant Woodruff Battery Production “With Plant Woodruff, we are further expanding our footprint in South Carolina and strengthening the close integration of battery and vehicle production,” Robert Engelhorn, the president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing said in a statement.
BMW Plant Woodruff in South Carolina.
Photo by: BMW AESC will still supply BMW's Gen6 battery cells, just from an undisclosed location instead.
The battery pack itself is among the largest we've seen on an electric SUV, measuring 144 kilowatt-hours (usable) in the U.S. and 141 kWh in Europe.
text:
Despite a rocky year for EV sales in the U.S., BMW is taking a massive step forward by bringing battery production stateside. The automaker will start mass production of the new iX5's high-voltage battery pack right here in the U.S. starting in December, at its newly opened Plant Woodruff in South Carolina, BMW said Monday.

Rather than relying on pre-assembled or imported packs from suppliers, BMW is bringing battery production in-house, a multi-billion-dollar effort that only a handful of automakers in the U.S. have attempted. It's more capital intensive upfront, but it's a long-term strategic bet that could help BMW build out a local supply chain, insulate itself from geopolitical shocks, and eventually bring costs down. Since the iX5 is built at the nearby Plant Spartanburg, BMW also stands to save on logistics and transportation costs by keeping battery and vehicle production close together.

Gallery: BMW Plant Woodruff Battery Production

“With Plant Woodruff, we are further expanding our footprint in South Carolina and strengthening the close integration of battery and vehicle production,” Robert Engelhorn, the president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing said in a statement. “This creates the ideal foundation for the next generation of fully electric BMW X models assembled at Plant Spartanburg.”

BMW said roughly 300 human workers and 250 robots will assemble the high-voltage packs, leaning on tools like virtual reality and AI to catch errors along the way. Japanese battery maker Automotive Energy Supply Corp. (AESC), now majority owned by China's Envision Group, will supply the cylindrical cells. AESC had originally planned to produce those cells at a site in South Carolina, but that project got paused last year amid a wave of battery project cancellations nationwide after the Trump administration pulled back EV incentives.

BMW Plant Woodruff in South Carolina.

Photo by: BMW

AESC will still supply BMW's Gen6 battery cells, just from an undisclosed location instead. The iX5's cylindrical cells stand 120 millimeters tall and pack 30% more usable energy than the 95 mm cells found in the iX3. The battery pack itself is among the largest we've seen on an electric SUV, measuring 144 kilowatt-hours (usable) in the U.S. and 141 kWh in Europe. That capacity translates to a BMW-estimated 435 miles of range. Despite the pack's size, it can charge from 10-80% in just 22 minutes thanks to a peak charging rate of 460 kilowatts.

How The Pack Is Actually Assembled

BMW engineers start by checking each cell’s voltage when it arrives from its supplier. From there, workers cluster the cells together and hook them up to cooling components, then weld everything together with lasers. Once that's done, the whole pack gets filled with a foam that hardens around the cells, locking everything into one solid block for protection.

Photo by: BMW

The pack housing is then sealed, and the Energy Master (basically the battery's brain) gets bolted on. The Energy Master also requires its own glue and seal so that it's properly locked in place and fully insulated from the outside. Every pack then goes through a final check before making the short 15-mile trip from Woodruff to the Spartanburg plant, where it will get dropped into the iX5.

What do you think?

Woodruff isn't the only place BMW is assembling battery packs. The automaker is also making them in Debrecen, Hungary; Lower Bavaria, Germany; Shenyang, China; and San Luis Potosi, Mexico. BMW calls this a “local for local” approach, assembling packs close to where the EVs themselves are built, which could give the automaker supply chain and logistical advantages for decades to come.

Site strengthens electromobility push in South Carolina The stakes attached to Woodruff extend well beyond one model.
